title: R4DGS: Referring Segmentation in 4D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 10 pages. Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026. Project page: https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/
summary: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.

Building on this foundation, recent dynamic Gaussian methods extend Gaussian primitives across time through deformation, temporal conditioning, or explicit spacetime modeling, substantially advancing dynamic scene reconstruction and free-viewpoint rendering luiten2024dynamic3dgs,yang2024deformable3dgs,li2024sgfs,wu20244dgs,yang20244dgsiclr . Among these developments, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) has emerged as an effective representation for dynamic scene modeling, enabling high-fidelity rendering with strong efficiency wu20244dgs,yang20244dgsiclr . Together, these advances establish Gaussian splatting as a practical substrate for dynamic visual modeling. At the same time, recent work has begun to study language grounding and semantic reasoning on Gaussian representations. In static 3D scenes, methods such as LangSplat qin2024langsplat , Gaussian Grouping ye_gaussian_2024 , OpenGaussian wu2024opengaussian , Dr. Splat jun-seong_dr_2025 , Segment then Splat lu2025segmentthensplat , and ReferSplat he2025refersplat connect Gaussian primitives with language or segmentation supervision. In dynamic settings, SA4D ji2024sa4d and 4D LangSplat li20254dlangsplat extend Gaussian-based semantics to time-varying scenes. However, many existing methods are optimized for category-level querying, scene-specific semantic fitting, or mask prediction, and are not designed for expressions involving temporal state changes, interaction cues, multi-target reasoning, or deliberately absent targets. This gap becomes critical when the query involves temporal states, relations, or set-level constraints. A practical model should handle expressions such as the cookie broken into smaller pieces, the complete lemon before the cut, all objects except the hand and the metal cup, or descriptions with no valid referent. These queries require temporal reasoning, entity disambiguation, set-level constraints, and uncertainty-aware rejection. Figure~ fig:task-definition summarizes the transition from conventional semantic querying to dynamic referring. Figure~ fig:teaser provides example visualizations of ReferGaussian for dynamic and multi-target referring in 4D scenes. To address these limitations, we define Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), which requires a 4D Gaussian system to resolve complex natural-language referring expressions in dynamic scenes and produce temporally grounded, set-valued segmentation masks. Recognizing the lack of a benchmark for this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA (QA denotes Query Annotations), which evaluates three challenging categories: 4D-varying queries, multi-target or reasoning queries, and zero-target or distractor queries. These observations reveal an abstraction gap between low-level Gaussian primitives and the entity-level units referred to by natural language. Dynamic Gaussian backbones provide efficient time-conditioned scene representations, but their primitives are not directly organized into persistent, language-addressable entities. Meanwhile, SA4D and 4D LangSplat enrich dynamic scenes with segmentation identities or learned language fields ji2024sa4d,li20254dlangsplat , yet remain primarily oriented toward segmentation-centric outputs or scene-specific semantic fitting. Consequently, temporal-state composition, multi-entity selection, and zero-target rejection are not naturally supported within a unified referring protocol. Motivated by this gap, we propose ReferGaussian, a training-free referring framework built upon 4DGS. Starting from a reconstructed 4D Gaussian scene, it uses mask-supported multi-view evidence to form persistent Gaussian entities, records their appearance, motion, relations, and valid temporal support in an EntityBank, and resolves structured referring constraints over this bank. MLLMs serve as the Refer-Planner for query decomposition and constraint extraction, while Grounded-SAM supplies 2D mask evidence. The final prediction is produced through explicit and inspectable entity-level selection, without scene-specific semantic training. Our contributions are summarized as follows: =-1 We formulate Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a novel task for language-grounded dynamic scene understanding involving temporal state changes, multi-target reasoning, and distractor rejection. =-1 We establish R4D-Bench-QA, the first benchmark for R4DGS, featuring structured query annotations and pixel-level spatiotemporal supervision to address the current lack of evaluation standards. We propose ReferGaussian, a training-free framework that organizes low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent entities addressable through language and performs constraint-aware 4D referring over an EntityBank. Related Work Scene Reconstruction. NeRF mildenhall2020nerf and its dynamic variants Park_2021_ICCV,pumarola2021dnerf,li2021HyperNerf,wang2021nsff,Cao_2023_CVPR laid the foundation for neural dynamic view synthesis. 3D Gaussian Splatting kerbl20233dgs replaced volumetric rendering with explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives, making real-time rendering practical. Recent work extends Gaussian splatting to dynamic scenes through deformation, canonicalization, or explicit spacetime modeling, including Dynamic 3D Gaussians luiten2024dynamic3dgs , Deformable 3D Gaussians yang2024deformable3dgs , 4D Gaussian Splatting wu20244dgs , Real-time Photorealistic Dynamic Scene Representation and Rendering with 4D Gaussian Splatting yang20244dgsiclr , and Spacetime Gaussian Feature Splatting li2024sgfs . These methods deliver strong rendering quality, yet their objective remains view synthesis. Our target is language-conditioned reasoning over dynamic entities. This requires temporal support that remains stable across rendering, downstream grouping, candidate ranking, and set-level decisions under ambiguous natural language. In practice, this difference is critical when multiple visually similar candidates coexist but only one satisfies temporal or relational constraints across a full event window. -Grounded Semantic Reasoning. Visual semantic reasoning has advanced across various domains. In 2D video understanding, several works explore semantic tasks such as open-vocabulary and referring segmentation wu2022language, wu2023onlinerefer, tang2023temporal, seo2020urvos, luo2023soc, jin2026vistamitigatingsemanticinertia, jin2026tirflowactivevideosearch, jin2026himachierarchicalmacromicrolearning . For static 3D scenes, current research explores two primary directions: open-vocabulary understanding and segmentation kerr2023lerf, peng2023openscene, qin2024langsplat, ye_gaussian_2024, wu2024opengaussian, jun-seong_dr_2025, ding2026extrin, ding20263dinstructionambiguitydetection, zhang2025cobgs, lu2025segmentthensplat, piekenbrinck2025opensplat3d , and referring expression grounding represented by ReferSplat he2025refersplat . In dynamic contexts, while SA4D ji2024sa4d and 4D LangSplat li20254dlangsplat enable time-sensitive language querying, they primarily focus on semantic segmentation, with limited coverage of complex referring understanding. To our knowledge, referring grounding in dynamic Gaussian scenes has not been systematically formulated or evaluated. Unlike existing methods that rely on scene-specific semantic retraining or learned language fields, ReferGaussian resolves referents through entity-level matching within a query-reusable structure. This training-free design supports robust reasoning over temporal states and set-valued targets through persistent entity records and explicit constraints. Models. Large vision-language and segmentation foundation models provide strong building blocks for language-grounded scene reasoning. Qwen3-VL bai2025qwen3 supports structured interpretation of natural-language expressions, while Grounding DINO liu2023groundingdino , Segment Anything kirillov2023sam , and Grounded-SAM ren2024groundedsam enable text-conditioned mask extraction. Recent multimodal systems liu2024improved,wang2024cogvlm,chen2024internvl further improve prompt following and visual grounding. ReferGaussian uses these models as modular components for query parsing and visual evidence extraction within a structured entity-centric pipeline. This decomposition improves diagnostic ability: query decomposition errors, mask evidence errors, and entity association errors can be analyzed separately. Task and Benchmark In this section, we first formalize Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS) and clarify its task setting. We then introduce R4D-Bench-QA, our benchmark for dynamic 4D referring understanding, together with its construction pipeline, annotation protocol, query taxonomy, and evaluation metrics. Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS) Given a multi-view dynamic video, a precomputed 4D Gaussian scene representation, and a natural-language query , R4DGS identifies the referred entities and produces their frame-aligned segmentation masks. The referent may be a single entity, multiple entities, or an empty set, depending on the spatiotemporal, relational, and set-level constraints expressed by the query. R4DGS adds three requirements to conventional referring: (1) Temporally varying queries specify an event stage or a state before or after a transition. (2) Set-valued and reasoning-intensive queries express conjunction, exclusion, quantification, or relations among entities. (3) Zero-target and distractor queries

title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
summary: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.

title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

Built on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs; ), WAMs have shown strong generalization to unseen tasks ye2026world,ma2026dit4dit , adaptation to new robot embodiments ye2026world , and skill transfer from human videos to robots dyna2026dyna2 . Their core idea is to leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors learned from large-scale in-the-wild video datasets chen2024panda,nan2024openvid by training a model to jointly predict future frames and corresponding actions. This allows the strong generalization capabilities of pre-trained video models to extend from future video prediction to robot control. Recent works have shown that WAMs can achieve competitive performance with a separate action decoder that generates actions conditioned on intermediate hidden states of the VDM ma2026dit4dit,dyna2026dyna2,qiu2026making,zhao2026faster . These hidden states are obtained from a single forward pass with Gaussian noise as input. This design substantially reduces inference latency by avoiding iterative denoising with large VDM backbones, making WAMs more practical for robot control. However, because the action decoder directly leverages these hidden states, policy performance depends on how well they capture future robot-object dynamics. In this paper, we aim to improve the control performance of the recent line of WAMs that use a single VDM forward pass for action generation. We start by performing an analysis of how well the VDM hidden states learn meaningful information to generate actions during WAM training. We first find that VDM hidden states generated from noise already capture information about future robot motion. Specifically, a lightweight probe trained on frozen hidden states can predict future motion primitives, with classification accuracy increasing throughout WAM training (see ). Moreover, these hidden states become increasingly similar to those extracted from ground-truth future observations at the same VDM layer (see ). These findings suggest that the VDM progressively learns to generate future video representations from noise. However, a clear gap in future-motion probing accuracy remains relative to representations extracted from clean future observations, suggesting that generating sufficiently informative future representations from noise remains challenging. Inspired by this, we propose Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context ( ), a framework for training WAMs to improve the future representations obtained from a single video denoising step for action generation; see the overview in . We train the VDM through self-distillation to align representations generated from noise with those extracted from ground-truth future observations, encouraging the model to capture richer future information for predicting actions. Specifically, uses a momentum teacher, implemented as an Exponential-Moving-Average (EMA) copy of the online VDM, to extract the target representations from noisy future observations at the same intermediate layer used for action conditioning. We further condition the VDM on a short history of observations, providing temporal context that helps the intermediate hidden states better represent future robot motion. As a result, reduces the future-motion probing performance gap to representations extracted from clean future observations and further improves structural similarity to them (see ). Notably, this closer alignment with representations of future observations translates into better robot control performance (see ). To validate the generality and effectiveness of , we conduct extensive experiments in diverse real-world robotic manipulation scenarios. We first evaluate on zero-shot environment generalization using a varied set of real-world manipulation tasks, including long-horizon manipulation, out-of-domain tasks, and object grounding. Our results show that consistently outperforms competing WAMs in these settings, improving long-horizon performance from 61.7 to 81.7 and out-of-domain task success from 10.4 to 52.1 at the 14B scale. We further evaluate on human-to-robot skill transfer by co-training the video model on human videos without action labels, including tasks absent from robot training data. We show that significantly outperforms competing WAMs, improving task success from 19.4 to 50.0 , while achieving 97.2 instruction-following performance. These results highlight that improves future representation quality and achieves strong robot control in both zero-shot generalization and human-to-robot transfer. We summarize the main contributions of this paper below: [leftmargin=*,topsep=0.0em, itemsep=0.0em] We interpret the VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in a single forward pass. We present , a framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context. We show that consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer. Related Work World Action Models. Prior work studies robot control via World Action Models (WAMs), which build on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs) and jointly model future observations and actions using robot data, allowing spatiotemporal priors from large-scale video to guide action generation~ shen2026videovla,li2026causal,kim2026cosmos, ye2026world . These models generate plausible future visual states to support action prediction, but iterative denoising with large video backbones incurs substantial computational cost at inference time. Recent WAMs address this bottleneck by decoupling video and action generation and reducing video denoising to a single step. Within this shared design, some works predict actions without explicitly generating future videos at inference by masking access to future video features~ yuan2026fast or directly decoding actions from video-backbone states~ li2026light . In contrast, another line of work conditions action prediction on future video representations obtained from noise in a single video denoising step~ pai2025mimic, ma2026dit4dit, qiu2026making, zhao2026faster . Our work follows the latter design and focuses on how to train WAMs to generate more informative future representations for action generation. Diffusion Models and Representation Learning. Prior works have shown that diffusion denoisers learn discriminative representations useful for visual recognition~ xiang2023denoising,yang2023diffusion,li2023dreamteacher . More recent work improves these representations during generative training, where REPA~ yu2024representation aligns noisy diffusion features with clean image representations from a pre-trained visual encoder, while SRA~ jiang2025no uses lower-noise representations from the diffusion model itself as targets. This direction has been extended to VDMs through alignment with pre-trained video representations~ zhang2026videorepa,lee2025improving,bhowmik2026moalign , while Self-Flow~ chefer2026self incorporates self-supervised representation learning directly into flow matching without an external encoder. Our work studies representation learning in WAMs, where intermediate video representations from a single denoising step directly condition action generation. AGRA~ qiu2026making adapts representation alignment to this setting by aligning these representations with features from a frozen visual encoder. instead uses representations extracted from observed future frames as distillation targets for representations generated from noise. This improves the future video representation used by the action decoder without aligning the intermediate video features to a fixed external representation. Method Overview sec:method:overview Let be an expert demonstration consisting of a visual observation , proprioceptive state , and robot action at each timestep , with a task instruction . Given expert demonstrations from a dataset, we train a policy built on a World Action Model (WAM; ) which repurposes a pre-trained video diffusion model (VDM) for joint video-action prediction with diffusion timestep . Here, the VDM predicts future frames from the current frames and a text instruction through the iterative denoising process at timestep . In particular, our method is motivated by recent progress in the WAM literature ma2026dit4dit,mimic2026fluxmimic,qiu2026making . They keep the VDM architecture unchanged and use a separate diffusion-based decoder to denoise the future action, with the diffusion timestep , For simplicity, we describe our method as a policy that predicts a single action and a single future observation. In practice, it predicts future actions and observations at once, which is straightforward to implement within the WAM training framework. where is an intermediate hidden state of obtained at , through a single forward pass from Gaussian noise . title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 14 pages, 4 figures. Project page: https://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab
summary: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR-targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store are available on the project page.

Introduction sec:intro Automating scientific discovery is a long-standing research ambition, traceable through early symbolic systems such as the Automated Mathematician~ wiki:automated_mathematician and DENDRAL~ buchanan1981dendral , the conceptual programme of AI-generating algorithms~ clune2019ai , and a contemporary line of work in which LLMs compose research ideas, write training code, run experiments, and produce manuscripts~ lu2024aiscientist,yamada2025ai,schmidgall2025agentlab,gottweis2025towards,liu2024aigs,tang2025airesearcher,feng2026internagent,song2026paperorchestra . The classical research workflow is bounded by an individual researcher's time and reading bandwidth, neither of which scales with the publication rate of an active subfield. Automating parts of the cycle could return researcher time to ideation and analysis. Computer vision is a natural place to test this: a single subfield now produces thousands of follow-up papers in a few years, and reproducing one published method often takes engineering effort comparable to producing a new one. We are not aware of an autonomous-research pipeline demonstrated end-to-end in a computer-vision subfield where reproducing a single prior paper takes weeks of expert engineering. Existing systems edit short LaTeX templates over brief training runs, rank free-text hypotheses without executing a training loop, or build experimentation on top of LLM-written reimplementations that have not been externally verified against the target paper~ lu2024aiscientist,yamada2025ai,gottweis2025towards,liu2024aigs,schmidgall2025agentlab,tang2025airesearcher,feng2026internagent,yuan2025dolphin,kon2025curie,jansen2025codescientist,li2024mlrcopilot,weng2024cycleresearcher . PaperBench measures this verification gap: across 20 ICML~2024 Spotlight and Oral papers, the strongest evaluated agent reaches 21.0 average replication~ starace2025paperbench . Without a verified reimplementation, an improvement claim has no fixed external reference: reported metrics may not trace to a measurement on disk, long-running agents drift from their objective as context fills, and comparisons are sometimes made against unspecified baselines. Table~ tab:capability-matrix summarises four common gaps: domain framework, verified baseline, full-loop refinement, and claim-to-log binding. Progress on this problem appears to require a domain-specialised research stack constructed on top of verified reproductions, rather than only improvements in generalist coding ability. full_text: Short title Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, and Wenzhen Yuan Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems. Manipulation, Tactile Sensing, Robot Learning, Visual-tactile Learning INTRODUCTION Manipulation is the process by which a robot physically interacts with and changes the state of objects in its environment. Because these interactions occur through contact, many manipulation-relevant quantities—including contact state, force distribution, slip, and local object geometry—can only be observed at the contact interface. Tactile sensing provides direct measurements of these interactions and therefore plays a critical role in enabling robust and dexterous manipulation. Research on robotic tactile sensing and manipulation has existed for decades. A central question throughout this history has been how tactile signals can be transformed into actionable information for robot control. Early research largely approached this problem from a mechanics-driven perspective, seeking explicit connections between tactile measurements, description of physical interactions, and manipulation actions. For example, tactile feedback can be used to detect slip so as to secure grasp, guide insertion and assembly based on force feedback, or measure local geometry for contact alignment. Although different approaches have been proposed—including analytical models, handcrafted feature extraction, and supervised learning techniques—the common principle is the use of explicit knowledge about contact mechanics and task structure to interpret tactile signals and guide robot behavior. In this review, we collectively refer to these approaches as mechanics-driven tactile-based manipulation. In recent years, the rapid progress of data-driven robot learning has profoundly reshaped tactile-based manipulation research. In contrast to mechanics-driven approaches, these methods typically do not require explicit modeling of intermediate physical quantities. Instead, they learn task-relevant implicit representations and action policies directly from data, often through imitation learning, reinforcement learning, or large-scale multimodal pretraining. This trend emerged alongside the remarkable success of vision-based robot learning, where end-to-end learning frameworks have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Consequently, a major research direction in tactile-based manipulation has become the integration of tactile observations into learning architectures originally developed for vision. This direction is particularly promising because vision and touch provide highly complementary information: vision captures global scene context and long-range spatial relationships, while tactile sensing provides precise local measurements of contact and physical interaction. Recent advances in sensor development, scalable robot learning, and multimodal foundation models have further accelerated this trend, creating new opportunities for tactile-enabled manipulation while also introducing new challenges. In this review, we examine tactile-based manipulation from both mechanics-driven and data-driven perspectives. We first discuss how tactile sensing captures the physics of contact and how tactile signals can be transformed into manipulation-relevant information through explicit reasoning. We then review recent advances in learning-based manipulation, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models that leverage tactile observations as part of large-scale multimodal learning frameworks. By bringing together these two perspectives, we aim to provide a unified understanding of how tactile information contributes to robotic manipulation, identify the connections between classical and modern approaches, and highlight the key challenges and opportunities that will shape the future of tactile-enabled robotics. Owing to the breadth of the field, we emphasize representative works that illustrate major ideas and trends rather than providing an exhaustive catalog of existing research. TACTILE SENSING FUNDAMENTALS sec:tactile sensor section Tactile Sensors and Signals Sec:Sensors The first step towards tactile-based manipulation is the tactile sensors. Tactile sensors measure touch, either in the form of a single point force/torque (F/T) sensing or the distributed information over the fingertip or an area of skin. Commonly seen output signals from tactile sensors include: [noitemsep, topsep=0pt, leftmargin=*] Normal Force, the component of contact force perpendicular to the sensor surface. It is the most commonly measured tactile quantity. Shear Force corresponds to tangential loads at the contact interface and plays a critical role in grasping and in-hand manipulation. The capability to measure shear force is much less common, but some modern tactile sensors, including magnetic tomo2018new,yan2021soft and vision-based designs ward2018tactip,yuan2017gelsight , can estimate local shear distributions. Torque is available for F/T sensors. For distributed tactile sensors, torque can be inferred from the spatial distribution of forces. Contact Geometry is typically achieved from the spatial distribution of the deformation or measured normal force across the sensing surface. Vibration in tactile signals contains important information about contact dynamics and is typically generated during sliding motion. In addition to extracting temporal features of tactile signals, some tactile systems explicitly incorporate accelerometers or vibration sensors to capture high-frequency signals. Auxiliary Modalities such as temperature and proximity. They are less commonly used in robotic manipulation and are therefore outside the scope of this review. Over the past decades, a large number of tactile sensors have been developed dahiya2009tactile . They vary in characteristics such as sensitivity, spatial resolution, force range, bandwidth, robustness, and manufacturing complexity. One rough way to categorize the sensors is based on the number of their measurement units. So, there are: [noitemsep, topsep=0pt, leftmargin=*] F/T sensors: only one measuring unit, but can typically measure 6-axis or 3-axis forces and torque. Installed at the wrist or fingertip . The force measurement is usually much more precise. Array-based tactile sensors: typically contain 4-100 sensing units to measure normal force with a spatial resolution of several millimeters. So a rough shape estimation is available but not precise shapes or textures. Vision based tactile sensors: using an embedded camera to capture raw images, so the spatial resolution can be very high. The downside is the bulkiness in size. Some sensors in this category are designed to measure the surface geometry of every image pixel yuan2017gelsight,lin2023dtact , while others track the motion of the printed markers schneiter1984optical,ward2018tactip , so their spatial resolution depends on the number of markers. One major challenge in tactile manipulation is the strong dependency on sensor hardware. The quality and availability of tactile signals vary substantially across sensors, often requiring sensor-specific denoising and preprocessing methods, and training data when using machine learning methods. As a result, algorithms and learning models developed for one sensor frequently transfer poorly to another, and the performance of one manipulation system highly depends on the choice of sensors. We will further discuss this issue in Section~ section:5-heterogeneity . Throughout this review, we therefore focus on reviewing manipulation methodologies based on how they are built on tactile signals rather than individual sensors. To abstract out the implementation differences, it is useful to adopt a unified physical view of tactile sensing. Tactile sensors consist of two components: a deformable contact medium, typically made of compliant materials such as elastomers or structures filled with air or liquid, and a transducer that converts the deformation of the medium into measurable electrical signals. Transduction mechanisms may be resistive, capacitive, magnetic, piezoelectric, or optical. Based on this description, tactile sensing is fundamentally indirect: rather than measuring contact itself, sensors measure contact-induced deformation so as to infer information about the interaction. Consequently, the differences among tactile sensors can be featured by the design of the contact medium and the choice of transduction mechanism. Tactile Simulation and Closing Sim-to-Real Gaps Sec:Simulation The growing adoption of data-driven manipulation methods has created a strong demand for tactile sensor simulation. Modern learning-based approaches often require large amounts of training data, while collecting tactile data using physical robots is costly and difficult to scale. Simulation, therefore, provides an attractive alternative for generating large datasets and training manipulation models in a safe and highly parallelized manner. It also provides a good platform for quickly evaluating the design of robotic systems at low cost. Accurately reproducing tactile sensor outputs while maintaining high simulation speed remains a long-standing challenge. While existing technologies cannot perfectly reproduce real sensor responses, improving simulation fidelity also comes at the cost of computational complexity. Since simulation efficiency is also critical for large-scale data generation, practical tactile simulators must balance accuracy and speed. Accordingly, current efforts in tactile simulation generally follow two complementary directions: developing more accurate and efficient sensor models, and designing algorithms to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. Unlike conventional robot simulation, tactile simulation must model both the contact mechanics between objects and the sensor, as well as the sensor transduction process that converts deformation into measurable signals. Most robotic simulators employ simplified contact models that cannot fully capture the fine-grained contact phenomena required for tactile sensing, while sensor noise, calibration errors, and manufacturing variations further complicate accurate simulation. title: KinoUAV: A Benchmark for Safe and Stable UAV Vision-Language Navigation with Kinodynamic Modeling
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have recently emerged as important remote sensing platforms, and UAV navigation has shown great potential in remote sensing applications. However, existing methods do not explicitly incorporate kinodynamic modeling or safety distances into trajectory generation, resulting in high absolute yaw rates, frequent collisions, and low navigation success rates, which limit safety and motion stability. To address this challenge, we introduce KinoUAV, a kinodynamic benchmark comprising a dataset and KinoUAV-Agent. First, we develop a hierarchical kinodynamic trajectory generation pipeline that drives UAV through acceleration actions. It uses waypoint chains from global planning and generates trajectories segment by segment under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints, reducing oscillations and improving trajectory stability. Furthermore, we introduce directional free-space distance (DFD) labels into the constructed dataset to describe the available clearance for safe motion decisions. The proposed KinoUAV-Agent predicts DFDs and uses them to generate safe actions, decoupling perception from action decision-making. This design enables autonomous obstacle avoidance and improves navigation safety. The benchmark incorporates the proposed Cruise-Seek task, in which the UAV first enters the target region and then searches for the target, reducing the difficulty of target search and improving navigation success. Experiments on KinoUAV show that KinoUAV-Agent outperforms existing methods, achieving the highest success rate while maintaining lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of kinodynamic modeling for safe and stable UAV navigation.

Introduction As important remote sensing platforms, UAVs are widely used in agricultural monitoring, infrastructure inspection, and disaster assessment shakhatreh2019unmanned, sun2024evaluation . Through autonomous navigation, UAVs can freely approach and observe specific targets, thereby demonstrating immense potential in the field of remote sensing. To achieve autonomous navigation in complex environments, Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) has emerged as an important research direction in embodied intelligence. Early VLN studies mainly focused on ground-based agents anderson2018vision, ku2020room, krantz2020beyond, qi2020reverie, chen2019touchdown, thomason2020vision, shridhar2020alfred, fan2023aerial . With the development of UAV simulation platforms, researchers have extended VLN to aerial environments liu2023aerialvln, wang2025towards, gao2025openfly, xiao2025uav , greatly improving the scale of scenes and the amount of data. However, existing UAV VLN benchmarks still suffer from several limitations in dataset construction. First, trajectories are commonly generated using discrete actions, waypoint interpolation, or loss-based motion constraints gao2025openfly, wang2025towards, jiang2026dynfly , without explicitly integrating kinodynamic modeling into the generation. Such trajectories may exhibit abrupt motion changes and limited control precision, making them unsuitable for learning stable UAV motion. Second, existing datasets lack effective supervision for autonomous obstacle avoidance. Current datasets often introduce additional information, such as multi-source observations, known obstacle positions, or explicit instruction cues for collision avoidance wu2025aeroduo, li2025skyvln, gao2025openfly . The substantial overhead of data collection and processing limits autonomous perception. Third, data containing detailed path instructions weaken autonomous exploration gao2025openfly , while target descriptions alone lead to inefficient search in large-scale environments xiao2025uav . Both types of data fail to provide guidance aligned with the current navigation stage, increasing the risk of missed targets and navigation failure. To address these issues, we propose KinoUAV, a UAV VLN benchmark built with kinodynamic modeling. First, we design a trajectory generation pipeline based on hierarchical kinodynamic A*. The proposed method performs path search according to different waypoint chains and uses acceleration actions to control UAV motion. It generates stable flight trajectories segment by segment under velocity, acceleration and jerk constraints. We then collect images and motion states at each sampling point. To support safe navigation, we introduce forward and downward DFDs to quantify the obstacle-free ranges ahead of and below the UAV. These DFDs serve as intermediate supervision, enabling the model to perceive environmental risks before making action decisions. This design decouples environmental perception from action prediction. Based on this data generation pipeline, we construct Main Subset and Auxiliary Subset: Auxiliary Subset uses randomly generated waypoint chains to plan trajectories, strengthening the UAV's waypoint tracking capability. The KinoUAV Dataset generates trajectories based on the start and target positions, enabling complete navigation capability. It is collected under the Cruise-Seek task setting to balance navigation guidance and autonomous exploration. During the Cruise stage, only target-region information is provided to guide the UAV for region-level navigation. After entering the target region, the task switches to the Seek stage, where target descriptions are provided for accurate target localization. This design avoids excessive path guidance and large-scale blind exploration. Furthermore, we propose KinoUAV-Agent, which adopts a hierarchical navigation architecture. The high-level waypoint planner predicts the next waypoint during both the Cruise and Seek stages. The low-level motion controller uses estimated DFDs for autonomous obstacle avoidance and predicts acceleration actions for waypoint tracking. Beyond existing VLN metrics, KinoUAV introduces absolute yaw rate to evaluate motion stability. summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.

In practical applications, VLN agents are often deployed under conditions that differ from those seen during training. Such deployment shifts may arise from new room layouts, varying illumination or different instruction granularity, leading to substantial discrepancies between the training and test distributions~ guhur2021airbert, gao2024fastslow, ko2025active, lin2021adversarial, wang2023learning . As a result, even strong VLN models often suffer marked performance drop when transferred to new environments, making online adaptation crucial for robust embodied navigation~ an2024etpnav, wang2023scaling, an2023bevbert, Wang2024GOAT, wang2026lifelong . Test-Time Adaptation (TTA)~ wang2021tent,niu2022efficient, niutest, su2024revisiting offers a natural way to mitigate such distribution shifts by updating model parameters on incoming test data. Motivated by its success in static vision tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation, recent studies have begun to extend TTA to VLN. However, existing methods~ gao2024fastslow, hong2025general typically rely on unsupervised objectives, such as entropy minimization, and perform policy updates at every step along the navigation trajectory. This strategy is particularly brittle in VLN, where navigation unfolds as a sequential decision-making process: an erroneous update at one step can change the subsequent state distribution, distort later optimization signals, and eventually cause cascading failures. Therefore, the key challenge in VLN test-time adaptation is not simply how to adapt online, but how to derive optimization signals that remain reliable throughout sequential decision-making. To obtain more reliable optimization signals, recent VLN-TTA methods have begun to incorporate human feedback at test time. FeedTTA~ kim2025test queries human whether each trajectory is successful or not, and uses the feedback as a reward signal to update the policy via reinforcement learning. ATENA~ ko2025active requests feedback only for trajectories with high entropy, calibrating policy uncertainty by boosting decision confidence on successful trajectories and suppressing it on failed ones. Despite their promise, these methods still suffer from two key limitations. 1) Inefficient Feedback Utilization: Once a trajectory-level label (i.e., success or failure) is obtained, existing methods generally use every obtained label to update the policy on the corresponding trajectory, even when the resulting adaptation gains are limited. 2) Mismatched Optimization Granularity: Existing methods use the same trajectory-level feedback signal across all steps, even though successful trajectories may still contain suboptimal actions and failed ones may still include locally correct decisions. This creates a mismatch between trajectory-level supervision and local action decisions being optimized. To address these challenges, we propose a ( ) that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. Our key observation is that the choice of trajectories and steps for feedback acquisition affects adaptation performance (as shown in Fig.~ fig:trajectory_selection_ablation and Table~ tab:ablation ). Based on this observation, we design a hierarchical feedback selection strategy that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization granularity. At the trajectory level, we prioritize trajectories with large fluctuations in normalized policy entropy, as such trajectories indicate unstable decision confidence and may benefit from external correction. At the step level, for each selected trajectory, we select the critical decision state using an entropy-gradient saliency criterion, which measures the sensitivity of normalized policy entropy to the action logits. We then query a single binary human feedback signal on the correctness of the selected action. Based on the queried feedback, we design a discrepancy-aware objective for policy optimization. We then apply directional entropy optimization: for actions verified as correct, the objective sharpens the policy distribution to reinforce the current decision. title: From Single-Actor Environments to Multi-Actor Event Worlds: Can LLMs Be Event World Models?
summary: World models help agents assess the consequences of their actions before acting. Many real systems, however, involve multiple actors who make their own decisions, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are only partially observed through event logs. We formalize these systems as event worlds and ask whether large language models can predict future observations from the log and the agent's proposed actions. We build complementary benchmarks from human Diplomacy games and real Polymarket trades. Our hierarchical framework compares prediction with and without other actors' actions, then tests multi-step rollouts, predictions for actions never taken, and usefulness to agents. Fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when all actors' recorded actions are given. With only the agent's action, models struggle when other actors strongly affect the outcome, and larger models and longer histories help little. This gap also limits multi-step prediction and agent decisions, with models overestimating plan success. Yet imagined experience and initialization from world models can still improve policy learning. Anticipating other actors' actions remains a central challenge for event world modeling.

Code: github.com/LingFengGold/EventWorld Introduction sec:intro World models simulate how an environment changes in response to an agent's actions~ hafner2025mastering,hafner2025training . Such models enable agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions before acting and learn from imagined experience~ ha2018world,gu2024your,li2026word . Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been used as world models in text, web, and tool environments~ wang2024can,gu2024your,ruan2024identifying,li2026word,zuo2026qwen,li2026bridging . These studies mainly use environments such as ALFWorld~ shridhar2020alfworld , WebShop~ yao2022webshop , and StableToolBench~ guo2024stabletoolbench . In these environments, the agent is the only decision maker, or actor. We thus refer to them as single-actor environments. They advance only through the agent's actions and return an observation after each step (Figure~ fig:world-model-comparison a). However, many real systems evolve through the decisions of multiple actors and are only partially observed through event logs. In healthcare, a doctor prescribes medication, but the illness continues to evolve and the patient may miss doses between visits. In a market, a trader places an order, but prices also change as other traders buy and sell, while their beliefs may change as news comes. In an online auction, a bidder makes an offer, but can lose the lead when someone else bids. In each system, we focus on one actor, the agent, whose decisions we aim to support. We call such systems event worlds (Figure~ fig:world-model-comparison b). They are driven by more than one actor, can evolve even when the agent takes no action, and are known only through event logs that reveal part of the underlying state. An event log is a sequence of time-stamped records of actions and observations. An event world model predicts the observation at a chosen time horizon, given the event log and the agent's proposed actions. The other actors' actions during this interval are unknown to the agent. An event world model can help an agent assess the consequences of its actions before acting, especially when testing alternatives in the real system is costly or restricted. Event logs record such systems at scale. However, prediction from event logs remains difficult, because they reveal only part of the state and leave the other actors' future actions unknown. Event logs also contain heterogeneous records of actions and observations. LLMs have the potential to understand these records. Knowledge from pretraining may also help predict how these systems evolve and how the actors behave. We thus ask: Can LLMs be event world models? To study this question, we construct two complementary event world benchmarks from human game records of Diplomacy~ paquette2019no and trade logs of Polymarket~ wang2026polymarket . We turn these multi-actor event logs into prediction tasks from one agent's perspective, separating its actions from those of the other actors. Diplomacy's rules engine additionally allows us to check the outcomes of actions never taken and evaluate agents beyond the recorded games. Polymarket tests prediction in a real market whose order book is unobserved and for which no engine is available to check actions never taken. To evaluate comprehensively whether LLMs can serve as event world models, we propose a hierarchical evaluation framework (Figure~ fig:framework ). Each level asks more of LLMs than the level below it. First, we evaluate how well LLMs predict future observations given the event log and every actor's recorded action (Section~ sec:q1 ). Second, we provide only the agent's action alongside the event log, so the models also have to anticipate what the other actors will do (Section~ sec:q2 ). Third, we test situations not in the event log, such as predicting several steps ahead using the models' own predictions and assessing the consequences of actions never taken (Section~ sec:q3 ). Finally, we ask whether LLMs help an agent act by planning, by choosing among candidate actions, or by imagining games for the agent to learn from (Section~ sec:q4 ). Our experiments show that (1) fine-tuning and more data improve prediction when every actor's actions are given. (2) However, given only the agent's own action, predictions remain less accurate, especially when other actors' actions have a large effect on the outcome, and this gap remains even with larger LLMs. (3) Rollouts accumulate errors, and fine-tuned LLMs predict the effects of actions never taken far less accurately without the other actors' actions. (4) The same gap affects agent decisions, with LLMs overestimating plan success and providing less help in choosing actions when only the agent's action is known. (5) Nevertheless, LLMs as event world models support policy learning through imagined experience and world-model initialization. These findings highlight anticipating the other actors' actions as the central open problem of event world modeling. Our main contributions are as follows. [(a)] We define event worlds and event world models, providing a unified formulation for predicting future observations from event logs and an agent's proposed actions in partially observed systems with multiple actors. We construct two complementary benchmarks and propose a hierarchical evaluation framework covering prediction with and without the other actors' actions, simulation of situations not in the event log, and usefulness to agents. We systematically evaluate prompted and fine-tuned LLMs, identifying their capabilities and limitations as event world models and providing empirical insights to guide future research. Related Work sec:related LLM world models predict future observations and support planning and policy learning in text, web, and tool environments~ wang2024can,gu2024your,li2026word,zuo2026qwen,chu2026agentic . We extend their evaluation from single-actor interaction to multi-actor event logs. Visual world models typically predict frames or trajectories sampled at regular intervals~ ha2018world,hafner2025mastering,bruce2024genie,hu2023gaia,montali2023waymo,wu2024smart , whereas event logs may record actions and observations at irregular times. Many multi-agent benchmarks generate interactions using LLM agents in predefined environments~ guo2024large,zhu2025multiagentbench , while our prediction tasks use human game records and real market logs. Event forecasting predicts future events from historical records~ shi2023language,halawi2024approaching,yu2026building . Our task additionally conditions on the agent's proposed action. Market and clinical simulators~ coletta2022learning,li2025mars,mu2026ehrworld are particularly close, predicting outcomes following trades or treatments. We build on these domain-specific studies with a unified formulation and evaluation, examining how other actors' unknown actions affect prediction and agent usefulness. summary: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.

Introduction sec:introduction Visual Language Action (VLA) models kimOpenVLAOpenSourceVisionLanguageAction2024a, intelligence VisionLanguageActionModel2025, bjorck2025gr00t, fang2026molmoact2 unify visual perception, language understanding and low-level robot actions into a single model, enabling them to generalize across embodiments, tasks and environments. Modern VLA models pre-train on large scale human demonstration datasets o2024open, khazatsky2024droid and utilize Supervised Finetuning (SFT) on smaller task specific datasets for task adaptation kimOpenVLAOpenSourceVisionLanguageAction2024a, shukorSmolVLAVisionLanguageActionModel2025a . If these VLA models are to be deployed on robots in real world environments, they invariably have to operate in the vicinity or even directly collaborate and coordinate with other robots and humans. However, the modren VLA models' ability to perform collaborative tasks with other robots or even humans in zero-shot remains underexplored. In this paper, we show that VLA models, even when finetuned on task specific single robot demonstrations, fail to coordinate with each other on collaborative manipulation tasks as most of the pretrained data of VLA models come from non-collaborative single robot demonstration data. Hence, the VLA models fail to learn to coordinate their policy execution with one another. We then show that finetuning on demonstration data that is collected collaboratively in a multi-robot manner does improve VLA models performance on decentralized collaborative tasks. Furthermore, we extend these results to zero-shot human collaboration as well. However, the data collection process for simultaneous multi-robot collaborative data can prove challenging due to either additional human cost for each additional robot or the lack of teleoperation interfaces to collect said demonstration data. To bridge this gap, we propose Co Gen: Collaborative Plan Generation for Decentralized VLA Training for Collaborative Tasks, a framework to autonomously generate collaborative data for multi-robot systems without multi-robot collaborative demonstrations. Our key insight is that collaborative robot demonstrations require the coordination and sequencing of each individual robot's sub-tasks to be conditioned on the successful sub-task execution and state of another robot. For example in Figure fig:main_fig , the arm on the right should only perform its sub-task of placing its cube when the cabinet is in an open position. Hence, any collaborative plan would need to sequence robot sub-tasks conditioned on both environment state and sub-tasks of other robots. Given a collaborative task prompt and environment state, our proposed approach, Co Gen, first leverages Visual Language Models (VLM) to generate a collaborative execution plan in the form of executable Pythonic function 10161317, liang2023code . We structure the plan generation process to be decentralized, where each robot utilizes a VLM to collaboratively propose and refine the generated execution plan using a collaborative Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) process zu2025collaborative, amanickapraveen2026playing . The resultant execution plans composes and calls on individual skills that are available for each robot and utilizes VLMs as a semantic verifier to check for sub-task preconditions for each robot skill execution. We then utilize the generated collaborative execution plan to generate collaborative robot demonstration data together with a human verifier to check for task success. Finally, we finetune the VLAs on resultant demonstration data. Each robot's VLA model is finetuned separately in a decentralized manner from its local data stream. We show that it enables VLAs to match the task execution success rate of VLAs finetuned on human teleoperated collaborative demonstrations. We further show that they also retain the match the for zero-shot human-robot collaboration across manipulation tasks. To summarize, our contributions are: We show that VLA models fail to generalize to simple collaborative tasks even when finetuned on task specific single-robot demonstrations. title: When One Step Is Enough: An Empirical Study of Euler Integration in Flow-Matching Policies
comment: Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.

Introduction Diffusion and flow matching models have now become the common choice for training robotic control policies for manipulation~ chi2025diffusion, wang2024rise,zhang2025flowpolicy,park2025flow,jones2025multitaskditpolicy , consistently outperforming simple regression/Gaussian baselines. To generate action samples, these models learn a vector field that drives noise samples, taken from a source distribution, to a target distribution. Of these, flow matching is now the dominant paradigm by virtue of its simpler form (solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) instead of a stochastic differential equation (SDE)). Many of the latest robot foundation models, in the form of vision-language-action (VLA) models, combine a large, pretrained vision-language model (VLM) backbone~ marafioti2025smolvlm,xiao2024florence,beyer2024paligemma,bai2025qwen3 , providing existing image and text understanding, with a flow matching action head~ shukor2025smolvla,zheng2025xvla,reuss2025flower,black2025pi05,zha2026lap,cai2026xiaomi . In flow matching policies, a velocity field is learned and generating actions requires integrating the learned velocity field, typically with an Euler integrator that evaluates the network times. Higher results in lower discretization error at the cost of increased latency, thus limiting control frequency, and subsequently hurting fluid motion in dynamic or contact-rich tasks. Recent works mitigate these issues by distilling the multi-step policy into a single-step proxy~ park2025flow , introducing distribution-shaping objectives that are expensive for large-scale VLAs~ li2026q0learning , or augmenting the flow matching objective to encourage straight-line flows that need fewer integration steps~ prasad2024consistency,yan2025maniflow0,frans2025one,geng2026mean . This multi-step formulation also necessitates backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) for gradient-based optimization of reinforcement learning (RL) objectives, which is costly and prone to unstable gradients. Due to the simplicity of its formulation, in practice VLAs are trained with the rectified flow matching objective)~ liu2022flow , where the target velocity along each training pair is constant, producing linear interpolation paths between source and target samples. It is not the case in general that the learned trajectories are straight, as intersecting linear paths produce curved learned trajectories, which in image generation degrades single-step sample quality~ liu2022flow . However, for robot control, given the current observation and state, the nature of the conditional target distribution may differ substantially from the image generation setting. Prior work~ pan2026much finds that, for control policies, the performance advantage of generative models over regression ones mainly comes from stochasticity injection and the dense supervision signal during training, rather than from modeling multimodality, which they find largely absent in robotics datasets (including the ones understood to be multimodal like |Push T|), likely due to their high-dimensional observation space. Concurrent work~ chen2026let reaches a similar conclusion for VLAs, but studies a single architecture, focusing on training hyperparameters on LIBERO~ liu2023libero and its variants, with a small real-world experiment. In contrast, we study six VLAs across multiple benchmarks, run a large-scale real-world evaluation, and analyse the smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories. We ask whether large-scale VLAs trained with the rectified flow objective and no additional regularization can be integrated in a single step at inference without loss of performance. We answer this question with what is, to our knowledge, the first paired one-step vs multi-step ablation of flow matching VLAs, covering six VLAs across multiple benchmarks. We evaluate six flow matching VLA models spanning M to B parameters (SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla , FLOWER~ reuss2025flower , X-VLA~ zheng2025xvla , ~ black2025pi05 , LAP~ zha2026lap , XR-0~ cai2026xiaomi ) on four simulation benchmarks (LIBERO~ liu2023libero , LIBERO+~ fei2025liberop , CALVIN~ mees2022calvin , RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin ) and a real world Franka suite~ zhang2026augmented . All comparisons use matched seeds and real world paired testing. We compare success rates through the two one-sided t-tests (TOST) equivalence test~ schuirmann1987comparison , analyse the difference in smoothness and diversity of the generated trajectories and also report a latency comparison. Results are summarised in Fig.~ fig:fig1-panels . Our findings are as follows: Step-equivalence is a factor of model scale, VLM pretraining and training maturity: The four largest VLAs show strong robustness to single-step inference across simulation benchmarks. and XR-0 are statistically equivalent within percentage points (pp) on every simulation benchmark for which a public checkpoint was available. X-VLA and LAP are equivalent on all but one benchmark each (Sec.~ subsec:sr-analysis ). Initialization ablations further suggest that pretrained visual-language representations favour step-equivalence, even without robot-action pretraining, and the difference between one-step and multi-step inference fades with longer fine-tuning (Sec.~ sec:ablations ). Similarly, for the real world, multi-step inference confers no consistent advantage in terms of success rate or trajectory smoothness (Sec.~ subsec:sr-analysis and subsec:jerk-analysis ). Longer task horizons expose greater sensitivity to inference steps: The two smaller models (FLOWER, SmolVLA) retain a performance gap that is larger on long-horizon tasks while their short-horizon performance is more robust to the number of integration steps (Sec.~ subsec:sr-analysis ). Importantly, additional Euler steps do not always help: the direction of the performance gap varies across the smaller models (Sec.~ subsec:sr-analysis and~ sec:ablations ). Practical payoff: For most current flow matching VLAs, multi-step inference does not improve performance over one step, enabling - lower latency at deployment (Sec.~ subsec:latency-analysis ). Taken together, these results reframe the conventional wisdom around inference in VLAs. While a growing body of work proposes auxiliary objectives explicitly to recover the single-step regime, we find that for the dominant class of present day flow matching VLAs, the single-step regime is already accessible without any retraining, architectural changes, or additional regularization. title: Adaptive Aerial Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning via LLM-Assisted Proactive Task Generation
summary: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.

Introduction sec:introduction Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach and operate in elevated, cluttered, and hazardous environments inaccessible to ground-based systems~ ollero2022past . However, changes in arm configuration continuously alter the mass distribution and inertia of the complete system, while joint accelerations and physical contact generate reaction forces and moments on the aerial base~ yadav2024modular . The flight controller must therefore maintain accurate trajectory tracking while adapting to changes in system response that are only partially revealed by available measurements. Conventional aerial manipulation controllers compensate for uncertain manipulation effects through analytically designed feedback and adaptive laws~ yadav2024modular,sharma2025impedance , whereas learning-based methods infer dynamics information from experience. Aco2~ jin2026autonomous learns a history-dependent context using contrastive supervision to distinguish payload conditions, while the controller in~ ujjawal2026learn learns multi-step dynamics residuals and adapts their predictions online for disturbance compensation. Their auxiliary objectives respectively organize context by task identity and train a residual predictor for a prescribed compensation law, while predictive-state methods use future observations to supervise the internal representation used for decision making~ venkatraman2017predictive,hefny2018recurrent . For aerial manipulation, similar instantaneous measurements can correspond to different hidden actuator and disturbance states that require different corrective actions. Predicting future measurement representations conditioned on recorded actions provides a direct training target for retaining these response distinctions in the history representation used by the flight policy. Since the available response information depends on the motion conditions encountered during training, repeatedly sampling fixed motion patterns can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored, motivating adaptive sampling~ jiang2021plr,mehta2020adr and task generation~ parker2022evolving that direct subsequent experience according to the policy's evolving performance. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. Inspired by the JEPA~ assran2023ijepa , ALMA trains its contextual flight policy by predicting learned representations of future measurements from recent history and subsequent actions, thereby supervising the information retained for control. Since learning this adaptation also depends on the responses encountered during training, ALMA uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze episode records, identify motion patterns associated with poor tracking, and propose new structures of arm motion that direct subsequent experience toward difficulties insufficiently addressed by the initial task distribution. Predictive supervision thus trains the context using measured action--response relationships, while task generation broadens the motion conditions that supply subsequent experience, connecting response learning with the policy's remaining tracking difficulties. Both components operate during training, while deployment retains the contextual flight policy to adapt to the changing effects of manipulation. In simulation, ALMA achieves the lowest mean position RMSE among evaluated controllers, reducing error relative to the strongest baseline by 24.5 under static arm commands and 24.7 under periodic commands, while ablations support the tracking benefit of predictive supervision and the generalization benefit of task generation, with base performance retained. The same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6 during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.
