title: SmolVLA-MoE: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables; conference paper prepared for IROS2027
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt2,brohan2023rt1,octo2024,kim2024openvla have emerged as a promising paradigm to address this challenge by unifying vision, language, and action within a single framework. Recent works such as RT-1~ brohan2023rt1 , RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 , Octo~ octo2024 , and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla have demonstrated that VLA models can leverage large-scale pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ liu2023llava,beyer2024paligemma as backbones to effectively generalize across various manipulation tasks. Despite their strong performance, most VLA models rely on large-scale architectures with billions of parameters, posing significant challenges for real-time deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. To address this limitation, lightweight VLA models such as SmolVLA~ smolvla2025 have been proposed, which employ a compact VLM backbone (e.g., SmolVLM2-500M) combined with a small action expert network for action generation via Flow Matching. This design significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining competitive performance. However, these lightweight VLA models suffer from a fundamental limitation: the action expert uses a single dense feed-forward network (FFN) to uniformly process all tasks. In multi-task robotic manipulation scenarios, different tasks (e.g., spatial reasoning, object manipulation, goal reaching) exhibit distinct action patterns that require different computational strategies. A single dense FFN is forced to encode all these diverse action generation patterns into a shared set of parameters, creating an inherent tension between model capacity and computational efficiency. Simply scaling up the action expert proportionally increases inference cost, negating the advantages of the lightweight design. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)~ jacobs1991adaptive,shazeer2017moe,jiang2024mixtral,deepseek2024moe offers an elegant solution to this dilemma. Unlike model compression techniques that trade representational capacity for efficiency, sparse MoE scales model capacity by maintaining multiple parallel expert networks while routing each input to only a sparse subset, keeping the active computation constant. This paradigm has proven effective in large language models such as Mixtral~ jiang2024mixtral and DeepSeek-MoE~ deepseek2024moe , yet its application in VLA models for action generation remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. Unlike approaches that replicate the entire action expert into multiple copies, our method operates at a finer granularity, replacing each dense FFN layer with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a learnable token-level router. This design enables each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation based on the input context, while keeping the attention layers shared across all tasks. We evaluate SmolVLA-MoE on the LIBERO benchmark~ liu2023libero , which provides four task suites (Spatial, Object, Goal, and LIBERO-10) covering diverse manipulation challenges. Experimental results show that SmolVLA-MoE achieves superior performance over the SmolVLA baseline on all four suites, while activating only a single expert FFN ( 100M activated parameters in the action expert) during inference, keeping the total activated parameter count at 500M---the same as the dense baseline. We further conduct systematic ablation studies on key design parameters, including the number of activated experts (top- ) and the shared expert weight, providing in-depth analysis of MoE behavior in robotic action generation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose SmolVLA-MoE, the first work to build a Mixture-of-Experts model on top of the lightweight SmolVLA architecture, maintaining the lightweight and efficient characteristics of SmolVLA under the same activated parameter budget. Building upon the AdaMoE~ zeng2024adamoe design, we introduce more controllable weight gating between shared and routed experts to balance pre-trained capability inheritance and expert specialization, and conduct systematic analysis of its impact across different task types. We demonstrate that SmolVLA-MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across all four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark while maintaining inference efficiency comparable to the dense baseline. RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 pioneered the VLA direction by fine-tuning a large vision-language model (55B-parameter PaLI-X) to directly output robotic actions as text tokens, demonstrating that semantic knowledge embedded in VLMs can transfer to robotic control. To this end, recent works have explored lightweight VLA architectures. ~ black2024pi0 proposed a flow matching-based VLA that uses a pre-trained vision-language model (PaliGemma~ beyer2024paligemma ) as the backbone and trains a dedicated action expert for action chunk generation. Mixture-of-Experts Models Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)~ jacobs1991adaptive is a classical approach for scaling model capacity through conditional computation, maintaining multiple expert networks and using a gating mechanism to route each input to a sparse subset of experts. The sparsely-gated MoE layer~ shazeer2017moe first demonstrated the scalability of this approach in deep learning. Subsequent works have advanced MoE along several directions, including simplified top-1 routing with load balancing~ fedus2022switch and large-scale top-2 routing~ lepikhin2021gshard . More recently, Mixtral~ jiang2024mixtral demonstrated that sparse MoE can match much larger dense models at a fraction of the inference cost. Two designs are particularly relevant to our work: DeepSeek-MoE~ deepseek2024moe introduced shared experts that are always activated alongside routed experts, providing a stable baseline; AdaMoE~ zeng2024adamoe proposed adaptive scaling adapters that decouple expert selection from expert weighting. In the robotics domain, the application of MoE remains limited. Existing approaches to efficient robot learning primarily focus on model compression: knowledge distillation~ hinton2015distilling transfers knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA~ hu2022lora reduce trainable parameters, and data augmentation techniques~ yu2023scaling,mandlekar2023mimicgen improve sample efficiency. title: WovenAnchor Matcher: Specialized Intra- and Inter-Image Context Modeling for Feature Matching
summary: Semi-dense local feature matching commonly aggregates contextual information before coarse-to-fine correspondence estimation. However, intra-image and inter-image aggregation serve different roles: the former should propagate spatial evidence within each image while retaining structured two-dimensional dependencies, whereas the latter should gather information from plausible corresponding regions while limiting noise from unrelated locations. We propose WovenAnchor Matcher (WAM), a semi-dense matching framework based on role-specialized context aggregation. WAM introduces two complementary operators. WovenMamba performs intra-image aggregation through horizontal-then-vertical state-space propagation, allowing vertical updates to operate on horizontally contextualized features and thereby encouraging a structured two-dimensional receptive-field bias. AnchorCrossAttention performs inter-image aggregation by using cross-attention to gather context from plausible corresponding regions across the image pair. It performs this exchange over local representative anchors that aggregate feature evidence within each window. On MegaDepth, WAM achieves 66.1 pose AUC@5$^\circ$, improving on the JamMa baseline by 2.0 AUC points under the same evaluation setup. Ablations show that removing or replacing either specialized component reduces accuracy, providing evidence that intra-image propagation and inter-image retrieval benefit from role-specific aggregation designs. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/mmaiLab/WovenAnchorMatcher.

Introduction Local feature matching is a core component of visual localization, structure-from-motion, SLAM, and image alignment sattler2018benchmarking,sarlin2019coarse,schoenberger2016sfm,murartal2015orbslam,hartley2004multiple . Modern semi-dense matchers estimate many correspondences from learned feature maps and commonly follow a coarse-to-fine pipeline sun21loftr,lu2025jamma,Li2025EDM . Before coarse matching, a context aggregation block updates descriptors using information from both the same image and the paired image. These two sources of context are not interchangeable. Intra-image aggregation should propagate spatial evidence while respecting the image's two-dimensional layout. Inter-image aggregation should instead gather evidence from plausible corresponding regions and avoid contaminating descriptors with visually similar but unrelated content. This matters because dense affinities can be unreliable under repetition, viewpoint changes, and local ambiguity. Existing matchers only partially encode this asymmetry. LoFTR-style methods explicitly separate self-attention and cross-attention, but both rely on attention-based token interaction as a generic aggregation primitive vaswani2017attention,sun21loftr,wang22matchformer,chen22aspanformer,wang24eloftr . JamMa improves efficiency by replacing attention-heavy aggregation with Mamba-based sequence modeling, but its JointMamba block applies a closely related sequence-modeling bias to within-image propagation and cross-image interaction lu2025jamma . These designs are effective, but do not fully tailor their aggregation structures to the distinct requirements of intra-image propagation and inter-image retrieval. WAM keeps the standard coarse-to-fine matching framework but replaces the generic context block with a role-specialized WovenAnchorModule. For intra-image aggregation, applies horizontal state-space propagation followed by vertical propagation. Since the vertical stage operates on horizontally contextualized features, the operator encourages composed two-dimensional dependencies rather than an additive combination of independent directional scans. We analyze this bias with a simplified linear model on a finite grid. This structured receptive field is important because intra-image context should preserve where supporting evidence appears, not only whether similar evidence exists somewhere in the image. For inter-image aggregation, uses cross-attention to gather context from plausible corresponding regions, but performs this exchange over local representative anchors instead of dense point-wise tokens bezdek1981fuzzy,Arandjelovic2016NetVLAD,lee2019set . Multiple anchors are formed within each local neighborhood, allowing different structures in the same area to receive different cross-image updates. Feature matching methods can be grouped into sparse, dense, and semi-dense approaches. Sparse pipelines detect keypoints and match descriptors Lowe2004SIFT,Rublee2011ORB , with representative learned systems including SuperPoint with SuperGlue and LightGlue detone18superpoint,sarlin20superglue,sarlin23lightglue . Dense matchers such as DKM and RoMa estimate correspondences over denser grids and can achieve strong accuracy at higher computational cost edstedt23dkm,edstedt24roma . Semi-dense matchers seek a balance by learning dense coarse features and refining selected correspondences; representative examples include LoFTR, JamMa, and EDM sun21loftr,lu2025jamma,Li2025EDM . WAM belongs to this semi-dense family and is most directly related to JamMa in its overall coarse-to-fine framework. Context aggregation for semi-dense matching. LoFTR introduced detector-free matching with self-attention and cross-attention over coarse feature maps vaswani2017attention,sun21loftr . Later methods improve attention structure, feature interaction, or efficiency while retaining attention-based aggregation wang22matchformer,chen22aspanformer,wang24eloftr . JamMa replaces attention-heavy aggregation with a Mamba-based module for efficient long-range modeling lu2025jamma . WAM follows this JamMa-like coarse-to-fine setting, but differs mainly in context aggregation. Instead of using a shared mechanism for both roles, WAM separates them into structured spatial propagation within each image and correspondence-aware aggregation across images. State-space models and compact cross-image interaction. State-space sequence models such as Mamba provide an efficient alternative to attention for long-range modeling Gu2024Mamba,dao2024mamba2 , and recent vision variants adapt scan-based SSMs to image grids Zhu24VisionMamba,liu2024vmamba . For image features, the scan order determines the spatial inductive bias; WovenMamba differs from scan-and-sum designs by composing the two scan orders rather than summing independent directional responses. For inter-image aggregation, dense cross-attention can mix information from non-corresponding regions, especially when noise or visual ambiguity increases their apparent similarity. This motivates compact local representations for more correspondence-aware cross-image aggregation. title: In-Context Learning World Models for Robot Dual-Arm Manipulation of Soft Garment with Partial Observations
summary: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.

Introduction Robotic manipulation of soft objects is fundamental to a wide range of domestic, service, healthcare, and industrial tasks, including assistive dressing kotsovolis2024garment and laundry folding hoque2020visuospatial , as seen in Fig front_page . Despite its practical significance, robotic manipulation research has predominantly focused on rigid objects bohg2013data , as soft-object manipulation remains substantially more challenging zhu2022challenges . Soft objects exhibits high-dimensional state spaces and complex nonlinear deformations, while their configurations are often only partially observable because of self-occlusion delehelle2024garfield . Moreover, their dynamics are highly sensitive to variations in geometry, material properties, and contact conditions. Humans address such challenges by forming internal predictive models acquired from a lifetime of data and experience. Such learned mental models can estimate hidden states, encode implicit knowledge of object geometry and material behavior, to subsequently predict the effects of actions on the current soft object state. This capacity for learning predictive representations from diverse experience motivates the use of data-driven models in robotics, as recent data-driven models have shown that large-scale predictive learning can extract transferable structure from diverse data brown2020language,radford2021learning, young2018recent, yan2024generative, choong2023jack . In robotics, learned world models have similarly proven effective for inferring latent state, forecasting future observations, and planning by simulating candidate trajectories within a learned dynamical manifold li2025robotic . Extending this paradigm to soft‑object manipulation is therefore a natural step. Garments and other soft objects exhibits strong nonlinear, material‑dependent dynamics that are hard to capture analytically but are well suited to learned predictive models that support dynamics reasoning. However, robotics models lacks the large and varied real-world interaction datasets available in language and vision. Collecting real manipulation data is expensive, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale, particularly for soft objects that require repeated resetting and exhibit substantial variation in geometry and material behavior. The first major challenge in building soft object world models is the high DOFs of soft object state space, where there exists many valid state configurations that occupy a complex manifold. In this space, small changes in contact point, geometry, or material parameters can cause different valid states with similar partial observations, further complicating state estimation. Partial observation from self-occlusion, folds, and camera poses routinely occludes task-critical regions of the soft object, forcing the world model to infer plausible unseen geometry. Selecting an effective state representation is therefore essential, as it must retain sufficient geometric detail for accurate prediction while remaining robust to sim‑to‑real mismatch. High-dimensional point-cloud representations are attractive because they preserve fine-grained geometry, map naturally to depth sensors, and empirically transfer well from physics simulators to real sensors when paired with appropriate domain randomization and generative conditioning tian2025diffusion . However, the data requirements for learning such expressive models are large and collecting extensive real-world demonstrations is expensive, thus motivating large-scale synthetic corpus generation in simulators like Isaac Lab mittal2025isaac . The second major challenge is dynamics prediction with rapid adaptation to material properties during inference. Predicting the dynamics of soft objects is challenging because deformations are strongly coupled to unknown material properties, grasp points, and the current unseen shape, where the same action can produce different outcomes 11236994 . In-context learning (ICL) provides a mechanism to reduce this ambiguity at test time. By conditioning the model on a short set of unrelated prior demonstrations, ICL infers material and shape priors without gradient-based fine-tuning vosylius2024instant . These demonstrations can also include diverse exaggerated dynamics, thus improving the model's ability to estimate dynamic properties, enabling rapid adaptation and more reliable forward rollouts. Accurate, context-conditioned world models can then be plugged directly into planning and control loops, serving as forward models, as action proposal evaluators or model-predictive controllers, therefore enabling robots to reason about long-horizon outcomes and select manipulation strategies that are robust across diverse garments. In this study, we aim to introduce and experimentally evaluate a Transformer-based soft object world model with test-time in-context adaptation for robotic manipulation. The framework reconstructs full object states from partial observations and predicts future deformations conditioned on planned actions and past estimated demonstration states. An in-context conditioning mechanism uses short sequences of estimated states to infer object material properties at inference without fine-tuning. To address data limitations and improve sim-to-real transfer, we train on a large-scale and diverse corpus of point-cloud-based soft object interactions, generated with Isaac Lab with randomized material parameters. We evaluate full-state reconstruction, multi-step action-conditioned dynamics prediction, and adaptation to variations in object geometry and material properties in simulation and real-world bimanual garment-manipulation experiments. Finally, we demonstrate sim-to-real transfer across multiple garment categories and material variants without test-time parameter updates. Related Work Soft Object Manipulation Manipulating soft objects such as garments remains a long-standing challenge in robotics, due to their high-dimensional state space and complex, nonlinear dynamics. Some works reduce the control problem by manually planning the manipulation trajectory and restricting learning to grasp‑point selection ha2022flingbot , an approach exemplified by methods that also predict manipulation primitive types alongside grasp selection zhou2025dual, avigal2022speedfolding . Unfortunately, these methods and some others that rely on visuomotor servoing osawa2007unfolding, maitin2010cloth , are constrained to the pre-defined skill trajectory. Data‑driven learning methods offer an alternative by enabling end‑to‑end mapping from unstructured perceptual inputs to control actions. Such methods like model-free reinforcement learning (RL) matas2018sim, jangir2020dynamic and imitation learning (IL) chi2025diffusion, fu2024mobile, ze20243d, pertsch2025fast, rouxel2025extremumflowmatching, rouxel2024flowmultisupport , has enabled robots to learn action policies directly from high-dimensional perceptual observations, such as visual inputs, without requiring an explicit analytical dynamics model. This property is particularly advantageous for robotic tasks involving unstructured environments and complex sensory inputs. Although model-free RL has been applied successfully to soft-object manipulation tasks, including cloth folding matas2018sim , purely model-free approaches do not explicitly represent soft-object dynamics or account for latent factors such as material properties and object geometry. This limitation can hinder long-horizon prediction and precise control of object deformation. Conversely, model‑based methods can enable shape control during manipulation through explicit dynamics models, but they require accurate state estimation. Such a requirement is difficult to satisfy under partial observability, and learning such models demands extensive data to cover the large state and action spaces characteristic of soft object manipulation chen2021ab . Recent and prominent research proposes to address the challenges posed by material-driven dynamics by learning soft-object dynamics models directly from empirical data sanchez2020learning, chen2022comphy, ma2023learning . The empirical data are often sourced from simulators mittal2025isaac , as collecting and curating real world data tends to be labour intensive. However, certain works have instead opted for differentiable simulators, where a small amount of real world data can be used to train for simulating realistic soft object dynamics via gradient optimization li2022diffcloth . Such simulators can then be used to generate an even larger corpus of simulated data that more closely match real world dynamics. title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
summary: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.

DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction. Introduction sec:intro World models are becoming a practical substitute for robot or simulator interaction in reinforcement-learning post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) policies. In this setting, however, their role is not merely to predict the next video frame: they generate the imagined rollouts from which the policy learns. This distinction creates an objective mismatch. A model optimized for one-step pixel prediction is not necessarily the model that induces the most useful policy-gradient update. The reason is that pixel fidelity and policy utility weight errors in different places. Pixel MSE penalizes prediction errors uniformly over pixels and time, including backgrounds, robot geometry, and visually salient but task-irrelevant regions. A policy-gradient update instead emphasizes the states the current policy visits and the actions whose advantages are large. A model can therefore be an excellent next-frame predictor while producing weak learning signals, or a worse predictor on average while better supporting the transitions that determine policy improvement. The relevant question is not only whether the imagined video looks right, but whether learning inside it moves the policy in the right direction. This mismatch matters because recent VLA post-training systems replace expensive robot or simulator interaction with imagined rollouts. At foundation-model scale, reinforcement-learning post-training can require millions of environment steps, so recent methods train a video world model from offline demonstrations and apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~ grpo2024 inside the model wmpo2025, vlaw2025, wovr2025, scvla2025 . Yet the world model is still typically optimized as a one-step video predictor. Diagnostic methods such as Policy-Aware WM~ policyaware2026 and ESNR~ esnr2026 show that pixel fidelity does not reliably track policy competence, but do not provide a training objective. RLVR-World~ rlvrworld2025 post-trains the world model with prediction correctness as the reward, improving it as a predictor rather than directly optimizing the policy update induced by imagined rollouts. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that trains video world models by the return of the policy obtained after learning in them. The inner loop performs a GRPO update on imagined rollouts generated by the world model; the outer loop updates the world model so that this post-update policy achieves higher return in the target simulator. The objective is therefore not pixel accuracy under the model's own rollouts, but downstream return in the environment that defines task success. DRILL has two operating points. DRILL-VWI (Visitation-Weighted Imagination) is a lightweight signed surrogate that replaces uniform pixel MSE with weights from policy visitation, group-relative advantage, and model confidence, requiring no additional simulator rollouts over a WMPO-style pipeline. DRILL-IMG (Implicit Meta-Gradient) estimates the downstream-return meta-gradient more directly by differentiating through the inner GRPO update with truncated Hessian-vector products and a small simulator-rollout batch. Thus DRILL-VWI is the budget-conscious drop-in update, while DRILL-IMG is the more faithful estimator when limited simulator interaction and BPTT memory are available. The two variants are connected theoretically: the core DRILL-VWI surrogate is the first-order Taylor approximation of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under standard local assumptions, and DRILL-IMG admits a non-asymptotic convergence rate with truncated backpropagation through the inner update. This explains when a local visitation- and advantage-weighted prediction loss can approximate the more expensive meta-gradient, and when longer-horizon trajectory effects make DRILL-IMG worth the additional cost. Across five public manipulation simulators libero2023, calvin2022, robocasa2024 and two foundation VLA backbones~ pi0_2024, openvla2024 , DRILL-IMG raises mean policy success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, while its world model has 17 higher one-step pixel MSE on the same training data. The gains are consistent across seeds, increase with rollout horizon and out-of-distribution shift, and remain complementary to prediction-correctness pretraining: applying DRILL-IMG to an RLVR-World-pretrained world model yields a further 3.2-point improvement on average. We also introduce the Policy-Utility Residual ( ), a method-agnostic diagnostic measuring the angular gap between the pixel-MSE gradient and the policy-improvement direction; across the objectives we evaluate, lower tracks higher downstream success. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*, noitemsep, topsep=0pt] We identify and formalize an objective mismatch in VLA world-model post-training: world models are trained for one-step pixel prediction, but used to generate policy-learning signals for imagined-rollout reinforcement learning. We introduce DRILL, a bilevel framework that trains the world model for the downstream return of the policy obtained after an inner GRPO update, and instantiate it as both a no-extra-rollout surrogate (DRILL-VWI) and a simulator-grounded meta-gradient method (DRILL-IMG). We show that DRILL-VWI is a first-order approximation to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient, provide a non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for DRILL-IMG under truncated BPTT, and validate the framework across five simulators and two VLA backbones with higher downstream success despite higher pixel MSE. We introduce as a method-agnostic diagnostic of the angular gap between pixel prediction and policy improvement, and show that it tracks downstream success across objectives. Related Work sec:related Recent VLA post-training systems use video world models to replace expensive robot or simulator interaction with imagined rollouts. WMPO~ wmpo2025 , VLAW~ vlaw2025 , WoVR~ wovr2025 , SC-VLA~ scvla2025 , Ctrl-World~ ctrlworld2025 , World4RL~ world4rl2026 , and World-Gymnast~ worldgymnast2026 pretrain the world model from demonstrations and then update the policy inside the learned dynamics. These methods differ in rollout construction, filtering, and policy optimization details, but the world model is still primarily trained as a next-frame predictor. Policy-Aware WM~ policyaware2026 and ESNR~ esnr2026 diagnose the gap between prediction quality and policy competence, while RLVR-World~ rlvrworld2025 and WorldCompass~ worldcompass2026 improve the predictor with prediction-correctness rewards. DRILL instead optimizes the world model by the downstream return of the policy after learning from its imagined rollouts; it is therefore complementary to RLVR-style pretraining rather than a replacement for it. The idea that a model should be useful for control, not only accurate under a prediction loss, appears in value-aware model learning farahmand2017value, grimm2020value and in neural model-based RL systems such as MuZero~ muzero2020 , IRIS~ iris2022 , and DreamerV3~ dreamerv3 . DRILL brings this perspective to VLA post-training with imagined GRPO rollouts. Classical value-aware objectives rely on a learned or bootstrapped targets; DRILL uses the group-relative advantage produced online by GRPO as a per-batch surrogate for downstream utility. Proposition~ prop:v1-is-v2-first-order shows that the signed advantage weighting in DRILL-VWI is recovered as a first-order approximation to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under a local score-compatibility condition, and Section~ sec:exp-ablations compares this approximation with a direct value-aware adaptation. Our analysis keeps the resulting truncation bias explicit: Theorem~ thm:v2-convergence expresses the BPTT bias as a function of the truncation length . The practical distinction is scale and target: DRILL-IMG applies meta-gradients to foundation-scale VLAs paired with 1B-parameter video world models, using a small simulator-rollout batch to train the world model for the post-update return of the policy. title: UniFlowWAM: A Unified World-Action Model with Visual Semantics and 4D Geometry
summary: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.
full_text: Experiments sec:exp Our experiments assess manipulation performance, robustness to distribution shifts, and the contribution of scene-level 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on an ALOHA-style robot for real-world bimanual manipulation. Experimental Setup sec:exp_setup -training data. We use a filtered mixture of three public robot-demonstration datasets; all are robot-camera recordings. RoboCOIN~ robocoin is a bimanual manipulation dataset collected on 15 robot platforms in residential, commercial, and industrial settings; we use 47 , 050 episodes from six of these platforms. RoboMIND~2.0~ robomind2 is a dual-arm and mobile manipulation dataset collected on six robot embodiments; we use 140 , 231 episodes from three of them, including Franka and UR arms. MolmoAct2-BimanualYAM~ molmoact2 is AllenAI's teleoperated bimanual dataset collected on a single low-cost platform, the YAM arms; we use 27 , 162 episodes. The combined corpus covers ten embodiments, with 214 , 443 episodes and 133.0 million frames. We sample 16-step chunks at three-frame intervals, yielding around 42 million training windows. We extract scene-level 3D flow offline with frozen Track4World~ track4world and encode its point maps and flow into latents using a frozen MotionCrafter 4D VAE~ motioncrafter . and training. Starting from LDA's released pretrained checkpoint~ lda , our model UniFlowWAM adds a dedicated 3D flow expert to the MMDiT backbone to incorporate flow as a third modality. Qwen3-VL-4B supplies visual--language conditioning through cross-attention, while DINOv3 provides visual prediction targets. Both encoders remain frozen during mid-training. We train on 48 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 1 , 536. Simulation Experiments sec:sim Benchmarks sec:benchmarks RoboCasa~ robocasa targets everyday household tasks for generalist robots. We use its GR-1 tabletop tasks: 24 tasks for a GR-1 humanoid with dexterous hands, observed by a single egocentric camera and controlled through 29 joint dimensions across the arms, hands, and waist. Each task comes with 1 , 000 demonstrations, 24 , 000 in total, or 6.0 million frames and 83.6 hours at 20 fps. LIBERO~ libero targets lifelong robot learning with a single Franka Panda arm. It contains 4 suites of 10 tasks each: Spatial varies the layout of the same objects, Object varies the objects to manipulate, Goal varies the goal within one scene, and Long collects long-horizon tasks. We use the no-noops release introduced by OpenVLA~ openvla . We evaluate in two settings. LIBERO itself is the in-distribution test. LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus perturbs the same tasks along seven axes, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background, sensor noise, and object layout, for 10 , 030 episodes in total. Following its official zero-shot protocol, we train only on LIBERO and evaluate on LIBERO-Plus. Post-training and Results sec:posttraining On RoboCasa-GR1, we train one model on all 24 tasks jointly. UniFlowWAM without mid-training starts from the released LDA pretrained checkpoint, and UniFlowWAM with mid-training starts from our mid-training checkpoint. Both follow a 500k-step cosine schedule with 5k warmup steps. The learning rate is for the action model and for the VLM, while DINOv3 remains frozen. We evaluate released and reproduced LDA checkpoints and both UniFlowWAM variants over 11 shared evaluation seeds (0--10), with 50 episodes per task and seed. UniFlowWAM achieves mean SRs of 54.84 without mid-training and 56.38 with mid-training (Table~ tab:robocasa , bottom). Both exceed released LDA (52.11 ) and reproduced LDA (52.76 ). UniFlowWAM with mid-training improves over released LDA by 4.27 percentage points. The gain concentrates on the tasks where released LDA is weaker. On the 10 tasks where its mean SR is below 50 , UniFlowWAM with mid-training improves on all 10, by 6.47 percentage points on average; on the remaining 14 tasks the average gain is 2.71 points. On LIBERO, we post-train one model on the four suites jointly, for 120k steps by default, and evaluate it on LIBERO and, zero-shot without adaptation, on LIBERO-Plus. On LIBERO, UniFlowWAM reaches 98.05 average SR (Table~ tab:libero ). Leading methods already score 97--99 on this benchmark; at this level of success rate observed, a difference of one percentage point is not informative, and we report LIBERO only to verify that in-distribution performance is preserved. LIBERO-Plus separates the methods more clearly. UniFlowWAM reaches 87.65 with its best evaluated checkpoint, and Table~ tab:liberoplus reports its success rates across all seven perturbation categories. The margin is widest under camera perturbations, where UniFlowWAM reaches 96.9 , against 76.6 for the strongest baseline in that category. Real-World Experiments on ALOHA sec:real . We use AgileX Cobot Magic, an ALOHA-style platform with two 6-DoF PiPER arms and parallel-jaw grippers. A top-mounted camera provides the main view, and two wrist cameras provide the wrist views. Both the proprioceptive state and the action command are 14-dimensional, with six joint positions and one gripper position per arm. . We consider four tasks that differ in what they demand of the two arms (Fig.~ fig:real ). Chili transfer repeats a single pick-and-place primitive, moving two chilies onto a plate. Cabbage transfer chains distinct primitives instead of repeating one, placing a cabbage into a pot and then covering the pot with a lid. Pen manipulation adds an articulated object and asymmetric arm roles, as one arm holds the drawer steady while the other places two pens into it in succession, after which the drawer is pushed closed. Towel folding replaces the rigid objects with a deformable one that has no pose to track, requiring two successive folds. After preprocessing, we retain 50 demonstrations per task and post-train a separate model for each task. At inference, each model uses the policy mode to predict 16-step action chunks. . For model with full objective setup as our default model, each policy is evaluated for 50 trials per task. We fix the starting conditions in advance instead of drawing them at random. Within a task we change one thing at a time, in equal steps. For chili transfer we keep the chili at the same spot on the table and turn it about the vertical axis to five fixed orientations. Each orientation is run the same number of times, and the plate position varies slightly across trials. The other three tasks follow the same idea along the factor that matters for them. All conditions stay inside the area the demonstrations cover. Every policy sees the same starting conditions, so the differences we report come from the policies and not from where the objects happened to start. We report full-task success rate and a process score, the fraction of milestones completed, scaled to 100. The milestones are those in Fig.~ fig:real , four for cabbage (grasp, place in pot, grasp lid, close) and chili (grasp and place each chili), six for pen (pick and place each pen, support the drawer with the right gripper, push it closed), and five for towel (grasp, lift, fold in half, fold again, press flat). Milestones are scored independently, so a trial that fails one but recovers on a later one still earns credit for the later one. Both metrics are averaged over trials, then over tasks. performance. UniFlowWAM reaches 87.0 average success with a process score of 92.3, against 68.5 and 77.0 for , 30.0 and 34.5 for DreamZero, and 15.5 and 17.8 for LDA (Fig.~ fig:aloha ). It is the strongest policy on every task. The two metrics also separate the failure modes. Averaged over the trials it does not complete, UniFlowWAM still earns 41 of 100 milestone points and earns 27, whereas LDA earns 3, so LDA tends to fail at the first milestone rather than partway through. The failure for LDA comes from severe arm tremor. Our reproduced LDA shakes strongly during execution, so the arm often knocks the object away before the gripper closes, and the trial rarely recovers. The two metrics diverge most on cabbage transfer. Its first two milestones handle the cabbage and the last two handle the lid. The round cabbage can roll out of the gripper while the lid is still grasped and closed, so UniFlowWAM succeeds on 80 of trials yet completes 92.5 of the milestones. Ablation Studies sec:abl -training objectives. We first ask what the objective grid contributes on its own, varying the objectives used in LIBERO post-training while holding the mid-trained initialization and the demonstration data fixed. The four variants form a nested ladder. The full grid uses all ten objectives, with 3D flow as both a target and a condition. The flow-as-condition variant drops the three objectives that predict flow and keeps the other seven. The no-flow variant also drops flow conditioning and keeps the four visual--action objectives of the base model. Policy-only training keeps the single action-prediction objective. Every variant acts through the direct policy objective and takes no flow input at test time, so the differences come from training rather than from the inference path. All four objective sets are first post-trained on the same 120k-step schedule. The reduced sets level off within this budget, whereas the full ten-objective grid is still improving at 120k steps. We therefore extend the full grid alone to a 200k-step schedule, and at 170k steps it reaches 87.0 on LIBERO-Plus. More objectives thus call for a longer schedule rather than lowering the attainable success rate. Because the simulated benchmark separates the objective sets mainly by training speed, we compare them on the real robot below, where at equal training steps the full grid clearly outperforms policy-only training. on the real robot. On the real robot, the four variants differ noticeably in success rate (Table~ tab:aloha_objectives ). Policy-only post-training reaches 76 on chili transfer, 76 on pen manipulation, and 72 on towel folding, while the full ten-objective grid reaches 94 , 90 , and 84 , a gain of 12 to 18 points on every task. The no-flow variant, which keeps the four visual--action objectives, closes most of this gap on chili transfer (92 ), but the gap largely remains on pen manipulation (80 ), where the two variants that use 3D flow reach 88 and 90 . On all three tasks, success rate improves overall as objectives are added. Relative to the no-flow variant, the 3D flow objectives add 10 points on pen manipulation and 8 on towel folding, the two more demanding tasks, but only 2 on chili transfer, the simplest one. the failures fall. Although the group contains few trials, a gap of 20 against 80 is large enough that we read it as a real difference rather than as sampling noise. Why that group is hard is visible in the training data. Fig.~ fig:coverage shows that the demonstrations are far from uniform. Most chili grasps cluster near the lengthwise placement, so the sideways orientation is the condition the model has seen least, and it is where policy-only post-training fails most. title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Project page: https://memory-before-goal.github.io
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).

Introduction sec:intro Whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) models~ wei2026psi0,bjorck2025gr00t,jiang2026wholebodyvla , paired with learned whole-body controllers~ li2025amo,luo2025sonic , have advanced humanoid loco-manipulation considerably. Yet most of them act on the current observation alone, ignoring temporal dependencies, and thus fail in dynamic scenes where objects change state or are hidden~ vanhoorick2023tracking,xia2026targo , moved or removed. Everyday cues are brief and seldom repeated: a guest waves from one of several identical tables while a waiter carries a tray, and when the waiter turns back, the hand is already down. Fig.~ fig:teaser shows this situation on a real G1: a cola stops on two seats and a sprite on one, the robot turns away to fetch the cola, and when it comes back the seats look the same again, so a policy that sees only the current view cannot tell where the cola stopped first. Loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is thus non-Markovian: earlier events determine later decisions, which calls for memory. We refer to it as pre-history memory: the record of the object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. Such memory is especially hard for a humanoid, whose head camera moves as it turns and walks, so cues leave the view, and whose memory must be updated causally while whole-body control runs. Even dual-system designs~ bjorck2025gr00t , in which a VLM planner acts as System~2, can reason over the history only if they locate the key frames. Existing memory strategies, mostly developed for tabletop arms, retain long frame histories~ torne2026mem,jang2025contextvla , which are costly and dilute brief cues; compress them~ shi2026memoryvla,wang2026nativemem , losing detail; sample frames at fixed intervals~ dai2026robomme , missing brief cues; or select event frames tied to the robot's own operations or learned from demonstrations~ zeng2026kemo,yang2026eventvla . As humans remember the moments when the things they care about change rather than every moment~ zacks2007event , we propose , an object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLAs. First, a frozen SAM3~ carion2026sam , a promptable video segmentation model, tracks the task objects in the head-camera stream, and we detect when they appear, disappear, move or change shape, compensating for the camera's own motion. Second, these object events causally select the key frames that fill an adaptive memory budget, stored as native backbone tokens along with mask-pooled object tokens. Finally, the action expert reads this memory via cross-attention and FiLM, so that whole-body actions depend on what happened, not only on what is visible. Existing humanoid benchmarks~ sferrazza2024humanoidbench,wei2026simple,wang2026humanoidarena,lin2026humanoidmimicgen keep the goal in view and do not test this problem, whereas memory benchmarks~ dai2026robomme,lei2026robomemarena are tabletop manipulation. We therefore introduce a memory-dependent humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark. Our contributions are as follows: We propose , an object-guided perceptual memory for whole-body VLAs, in which object events, rather than even sampling, select the key frames of an adaptive budget, read together with object tokens. We introduce HuMeGo, a memory-dependent humanoid loco-manipulation benchmark: six simulated tasks covering object, spatial and temporal memory, where the scene ends the cue and decisions are scored apart from manipulation, and six real-world G1 tasks, where the robot also turns away from the cue. keeps the right frames rather than more frames, outperforms memoryless and uniform-memory baselines in decisions and success, helps even on SIMPLE, and carries over to a real G1. Related Work sec:related Whole-Body Humanoid Loco-Manipulation VLAs sec:related_wbc Whole-body humanoid control uses learned whole-body controllers such as HOVER~ he2025hover , AMO~ li2025amo and SONIC~ luo2025sonic , and demonstrations are collected by whole-body teleoperation~ ze2025twist . On top of such controllers, vision-language-action (VLA) policies map images and instructions to whole-body actions. Generalist VLAs such as ~ black2025pi05 generalize across scenes and are adapted to whole-body action spaces; GR00T~ bjorck2025gr00t is an open foundation model for humanoids trained on real, synthetic and video data; ~ wei2026psi0 pre-trains on human egocentric video and then fine-tunes on a smaller amount of real humanoid data; and WholeBodyVLA~ jiang2026wholebodyvla learns a unified latent action space for loco-manipulation. These policies differ in their data, action spaces and controllers, but all of them condition on the current observation and a short proprioceptive history, so an event that has left the camera's view can no longer affect their actions. Memory has so far been added mostly to robots that do not walk, e.g.\ EgoMI~ yu2025egomi keeps past views for a wheeled semi-humanoid with an actuated head and SOMA~ li2026soma builds a spatial memory from a movable head camera; to our knowledge, no prior work studies memory for whole-body loco-manipulation, where the robot's own walking and turning move cues out of view. Concurrent work, POT-VLA~ ren2026closing , keeps a 3D record of where each task object is now but not what happened before; keeps the past views in which objects changed. Memory and Datasets for Robot Policies sec:related_mem Memory mechanisms. Memory for robot policies has been studied mainly on tabletop arms with fixed or wrist cameras~ dai2026robomme,shi2026memoryvla,fang2025sam2act,sridhar2026memer , and on mobile and navigation agents~ cheng2025navila . Long frame histories~ jang2025contextvla,torne2026mem grow in cost and dilute a short cue; compression into gist tokens~ wang2026nativemem or memory banks and object slots~ shi2026memoryvla,chung2026rethinking keeps the cost fixed but can lose the detail a decision needs; frame selection keeps native detail at a fixed budget, by uniform sampling~ dai2026robomme , retrieval~ sridhar2026memer or events~ zeng2026kemo,yang2026eventvla . title: An Introduction to World Models for Generalist Agents
summary: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.

" The most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible "---Albert Einstein Introduction A long-standing goal of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) is to develop generalist agents that can perceive, reason, and act effectively across diverse environments and tasks~ reed2022generalist . Achieving this requires more than recognizing patterns in observations or reproducing actions from demonstrations. An agent must acquire knowledge about how the world works, how it changes, and how its actions influence future outcomes. Recently, world models have emerged as a popular and promising direction toward this goal. Advances in generative modeling, video prediction, robotics, and large language models (LLMs) have stimulated growing interest in building agents that can learn how the world works and use this knowledge to guide their actions bruce2024genie,ding2025understanding . This direction is particularly relevant to physical intelligence, where agents must understand and interact with the physical world across diverse tasks and embodiments~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . The growing availability of images, videos, and robotic interaction data provides new opportunities to acquire such world knowledge at scale~ grauman2022ego4d,o2024open . Despite this growing interest, the meaning of world model remains surprisingly ambiguous. The term has been used to describe a wide range of models, including predictive dynamics models, generative video models, learned simulators, and models that jointly predict future observations and actions. Even action policies can be viewed as implicitly containing a model of the world. These approaches differ substantially in their learning objectives, representations, architectures, and intended applications. The idea of learning internal models of the environment has a long history in AI and control. Model-based control and reinforcement learning have traditionally used models of system dynamics to predict the consequences of actions and support planning sutton1991dyna,sutton1998reinforcement . The term world model gained renewed attention with a series of recent work ha2018recurrent,hafner2019learning,hafner2019dream,lecun2022path . More recently, advances in video generation~ liu2024sorareviewbackgroundtechnology and world-action models~ ye2026world have further blurred the boundaries between predicting the world, simulating interactions, and generating actions. To clarify these concepts, it is useful to consider the two words in world model. A model, broadly speaking, is an informative representation of an object or system, constructed to describe, understand, or predict its behavior wikipedia_model . A model need not reproduce every detail of reality, but rather capture selected properties relevant to its intended purpose. A mathematical model of atmospheric dynamics, for example, captures aspects of the physical system relevant to weather forecasting. A related concept is simulation, which involves constructing a model of a system and conducting experiments with that model to understand its behavior or evaluate alternative strategies~ shannon1975systems . The word world highlights a broader ambition: learning knowledge that is useful across diverse environments and tasks, rather than modeling a narrowly specified system for a single application. For generalist agents, such knowledge may include the structure of environments, the evolution of their states, the consequences of actions, and the relationships between observations, actions, and outcomes. Importantly, this does not require a world model to capture every aspect of the environment. Different models may represent different components of the world, at different levels of abstraction, depending on what information is useful for prediction and decision-making. In this paper, we study world models from the perspective of designing generalist agents, whose objective is to maximize rewards across diverse environments and tasks. We formalize this setting using partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs)~ sutton1998reinforcement , which provide a unified framework for describing environment states, observations, actions, and dynamics. We adopt a broad definition of a world model as a learned representation that captures aspects of an environment's structure, state, or dynamics to support understanding, prediction, or decision-making. Under this perspective, different approaches to world modeling can be characterized by the environmental knowledge they capture and the relationships they learn. For example, observation-space world models predict future observations, while latent-space models learn representations and their evolution. Passive predictive models learn temporal regularities from observations ~ gao2022simvp , whereas action-conditioned models predict how the environment responds to actions ~ hafner2019learning . A policy, in contrast, selects actions based on the available information and task. Although policy learning does not necessarily involve explicit world modeling, effective decision-making often requires implicitly capturing relevant aspects of the environment and its dynamics. Thus, world modeling and policy learning represent distinct but closely related capabilities, both relying on knowledge of the world to varying degrees to support effective behavior. As illustrated in , they can leverage diverse data sources and shared representations, while learned world models can further support inference-time planning and policy improvement through simulated experience. More fundamentally, world modeling and policy learning can be connected through a unified probabilistic perspective. A policy predicts which action to take given the current context, a forward dynamics model predicts the consequences of an action, and an inverse dynamics model predicts the action associated with an observed transition. These can be viewed as different conditional distributions derived from a joint distribution over actions and future observations. This perspective motivates recent world-action models, which integrate world prediction and action generation through shared representations, joint learning objectives, or interacting generative architectures~ wu2024unleashing,ye2026world . LLMs provide another intriguing perspective. Trained on internet-scale text through next-token prediction, followed by fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, LLMs have demonstrated broad capabilities in reasoning, tool use, and interactive problem-solving~ yao2023react . Although next-token prediction is not explicitly designed for learning environment dynamics, the training data contains extensive descriptions of events, actions, interactions, and their consequences. Depending on the conditioning context and prediction target, the same autoregressive objective can implicitly provide supervision for policies, forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and other forms of prediction. This suggests that general-purpose predictive learning may acquire implicit representations of the world ~ li2022emergent , which can be further strengthened through interaction-based training~ chae2025web,gu2025webdreamer,zhang2026earlyexperience . Our goal in this paper is to provide a unified introduction to world models from the perspective of learning generalist agents. Rather than focusing on specific architectures or implementation details, we emphasize the underlying modeling principles, aiming to clarify the relationships among different approaches to world modeling, their learning objectives, and their roles in supporting decision-making. Inspired by the success of large-scale predictive learning in LLMs, we also highlight how these principles may enable generalist agents to leverage diverse data sources, ranging from passive videos and egocentric human observations to action-labeled demonstrations and interaction trajectories. By extracting complementary learning signals from such data, world modeling and policy learning may jointly support the acquisition of transferable knowledge across environments, tasks, and embodiments. We do not attempt an exhaustive survey of the rapidly growing literature, for which we refer readers to several recent surveys~ ding2025understanding,hou2026world . Instead, we focus on representative approaches that illustrate the key concepts and connections. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first formulate the generalist-agent problem using the POMDP framework in . Following the perspective of~ recht2019tour , we then draw connections to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning in . In , we introduce policy learning and different approaches to world modeling, highlighting their learning objectives, representations, and roles in supporting decision-making. Finally, we conclude in , we conclude with a discussion of some other key challenges and future directions, including generalization across embodiments, scaling data and learning signals, state and action representations, high-level reasoning, and the evaluation of world models for decision-making. A central research question is how agents can acquire transferable knowledge from heterogeneous data and interaction experience to support effective decision-making and generalization. title: FocusVLA: Future-Intent Guided Dynamic View Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $π_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $π_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.

Introduction Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ kim2025fine, intelligence2025pi_, black2024pi_0, liu2025rdt, bjorck2025gr00t, wu2026pragmatic, kim2024openvla, yang2025instructvla, fan2025long, qu2025spatialvla, zhang2025ta have shown strong potential for generalist robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. In real-world manipulation, robust action generation often requires visual observations that can handle occlusions, viewpoint variations, and fine-grained interactions. Therefore, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary visual information~ seo2023multi, lan2025bfa, jangir2022look : third-person cameras provide global scene context for target localization and motion planning, while wrist cameras provide local cues for alignment, grasping, and contact-rich execution. However, existing VLA models typically fuse visual observations with language instructions and robot states into a fixed context for action generation. Although this paradigm effectively integrates multimodal information, it rarely considers that the policy's visual dependency may change across manipulation stages. Our empirical analysis further shows that, under the static fusion paradigm, the model is prone to view-dependency inertia during action generation: the policy may develop a strong reliance on a particular view at an early task stage according to the current manipulation demand. Although such reliance may be reasonable at the early stage, the lack of explicit awareness of task progress causes the early-formed observation preference to persist into later stages, making it difficult for the policy to dynamically adjust the contributions of different views to action generation according to changing manipulation requirements. This phenomenon suggests that improving multi-view utilization requires not only fusing multi-view information, but also enabling the policy to dynamically select and coordinate different view observations during action execution. Motivated by these observations, we aim to mitigate the stage-view misalignment caused by static fusion. Achieving this goal requires answering two key questions: (1) how can a VLA policy acquire a representation that reflects task progress and use it to infer the visual requirements of upcoming manipulation stages? (2) how can such a representation be transformed into effective multi-view routing signals without disrupting the pretrained VLA backbone? To answer these questions, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware dynamic view routing framework for multi-view VLA policies, as shown in Fig.~ fig:overview . FocusVLA predicts future action intent from multimodal observations and short-term action history, and uses it to generate action-step-wise routing weights that dynamically coordinate visual features from different views during action generation. The framework is non-invasive, requiring no modification to the visual encoder, language model, or action-generation backbone. We evaluate FocusVLA in both simulation and real-world settings. The simulation experiments cover all 50 RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin tasks, and the real-world experiments include 6 representative manipulation tasks with diverse object configurations, viewpoint variations, and interaction requirements. Results show that FocusVLA consistently outperforms static multi-view fusion baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating stage-view misalignment and improving policy adaptability. In summary, our contributions are: (1) We identify and quantify a temporal failure in static multi-view VLA policies: view dependence formed at earlier stages persists after visual requirements change, causing stage--view misalignment. (2) We propose FocusVLA, a task-progress-aware visual modulation framework that converts future action intent into action-step-wise view-routing weights for non-invasive dynamic multi-view modulation. (3) We evaluate FocusVLA on all 50 RoboTwin simulation tasks and 6 real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved adaptability and robustness over static multi-view baselines. Related Works Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation for robotic control~ brohan2022rt, zitkovich2023rt, team2024octo, wu2024unleashing, cheang2024gr, wen2025dexvla, shukor2025smolvla, team2025gemini, zhao2025cot, zhang2026dreamvla, lu2025vla . Recent models have improved generalist manipulation through diverse action generation paradigms, model scaling, and data scaling~ o2024open, khazatsky2024droid . However, most existing VLA models still follow a relatively fixed perception-to-action pipeline. As shown in Fig.~ fig:normal_arc , visual observations are first encoded into image tokens or visual features, fused with language instructions and robot states, and then provided as context to the action generation module~ intelligence2025pi_, black2024pi_0, kim2024openvla, zitkovich2023rt . Unlike prior works that mainly improve action decoders or scale VLA backbones, FocusVLA introduces a lightweight, architecture-agnostic view-routing module on the action-generation side. By predicting future action intent, FocusVLA dynamically modulates global and local visual contexts, enabling stage-aware multi-view adaptation without modifying existing VLA architectures. Multi-View Perception and Dynamic Visual Routing. Multi-view perception provides complementary information for robotic manipulation~ seo2023multi, jangir2022look : third-person views capture global scene context, while wrist views provide fine-grained hand--object interaction cues. Existing methods exploit such observations through representation learning, 3D reconstruction, feature aggregation, cross-attention, or perspective-adaptive fusion~ gervet2023act3d, acar2023visual, lin2021multi, akinola2020learning, chen2025temporal, mao2025omnid, ke20243d ; recent VLA-oriented works further demonstrate the value of multi-view inputs for action generation~ bian2025vla, fan2026peafowl, li2025uni, sarowar2026gst . Most methods nevertheless adopt fixed view organization or generic fusion. BFA~ lan2025bfa addresses redundancy from equally treating current multi-view features by predicting vision-based view weights and fusing the features before an imitation policy. title: FastHarness: Experience-Driven Review Scheduling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Agentic robot systems combine language-model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision of a π0.5 policy. A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions. The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval. On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT-as-Policy (π0.5 + GPT-6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.

GPT-as-Policy follows this approach by pairing intelligence2025pi_ with GPT-6 Astra su2026astra . Frequent model calls, however, can make execution slow and costly. Reviewing every action chunk repeats this overhead even in task stages that the policy has already completed reliably. Errors require a different response: a missed grasp or dropped object may need several rounds of correction before execution can continue. Repeated task execution provides evidence for distinguishing these situations. The challenge is to use that evidence to reduce redundant review while retaining the supervision needed for recovery. We introduce , an experience-driven harness that uses reviewed outcomes to decide when model supervision is needed (Figure~ fig:teaser ). title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
summary: Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions. Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions. However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics. Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction. The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions. On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo. Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
