Introduction Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions, supporting policy evaluation and model-based planning~ yang2024unisim,wu2024ivideogpt . Accurate simulation requires modeling robot motion and resulting scene changes. Latent action models encode visual transitions as proxy actions~ bruce2024genie,ye2025lapa , allowing world models to learn dynamics from large-scale videos without explicit action annotations~ gao2026dreamdojo . These latent actions are learned through future-observation reconstruction, with the current observation providing visual context~ gao2025adaworld,liang2026clam . For action-conditioned simulation, inferred latent actions serve as supervision for mapping robot controls into the learned latent action space. Learning this mapping is challenging since reconstruction objectives encourage latent actions to encode robot motion together with object responses and other scene changes~ nikulin2025distractors,zhang2025lamlearn . For example, similar end-effector motions may produce different object responses under different contact states~ gu2026geniworld,xu2026kinema4d , introducing scene-dependent variation beyond robot motion into the adaptation target. These interaction outcomes are useful for world modeling, since accurate simulation requires predicting how robot motion affects the surrounding scene. This motivates a dedicated kinematic component for action adaptation, together with a residual component retaining complementary transition information for dynamics learning. To this end, we propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling. Robot skeletons describe robot configuration and motion while abstracting scene appearance. Related robot world models use skeleton sequences or kinematic renderings as direct conditioning signals for generation~ wang2025vap,wu2026oscar,xu2026kinema4d . SkeLAM uses paired RGB and skeleton transitions to learn kinematic and residual components from RGB observations. Skeleton supervision grounds the kinematic latent in robot motion, while the residual latent supplies complementary information for RGB reconstruction. Together, the two components jointly support reconstruction, providing a dedicated target for action adaptation while retaining information for dynamics learning. During representation learning, skeletons supervise the RGB latents, while the deployed interface uses RGB observations and robot actions. We further introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction, which replaces the RGB kinematic latent with its paired skeleton counterpart while retaining the RGB residual. Reconstructing the same transition under this substitution encourages compatible motion conditioning in the RGB decoder, extending cross-modal correspondence beyond alignment in latent space. The world model learns from both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout prepares it for the zero-residual condition used at deployment. A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions. At inference, generation uses the current observation and robot actions. To assess motion accuracy and visual fidelity, we evaluate SkeLAM on DROID~ khazatsky2024droid . Compared with DreamDojo, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5 and LPIPS by 11.1 . Motion probing shows that the kinematic component approaches the performance of the concatenated representation with half the latent dimensions, while latent interventions and component ablations support its role in generation. Qualitative results further demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts. Open-loop policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions. title: Point-Level Refinable Semantic Mapping for Spatial Understanding
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

Introduction sec:intro Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for robot autonomy wang2025imperative by grounding open-ended semantic concepts in 3D space rotondi20263d . They enable robots to localize task-relevant objects, reason about object relationships, and maintain persistent spatial context for embodied tasks, e.g., vision-language navigation~ zhang2024vision and mobile manipulation~ du2026iflax . Recent open-vocabulary mapping systems~ gu2024conceptgraphs, Werby-RSS-24, maggio2024clio construct object-centric 3D semantic maps by integrating RGB-D observations with open-vocabulary perception models. However, real-world robotic deployment requires long-term operation in dynamic environments, where objects are frequently moved, removed, or rearranged. Existing methods are largely designed for static scenes and rely on an append-only point integration strategy: newly observed points are continuously added to object instances, while previously integrated points are rarely revisited or revised. Several recent methods have extended semantic mapping to dynamic environments by detecting object changes and updating object-level map representations~ Schmid-RSS24-Khronos,tang2025openin,jiang2025dualmap . For example, Khronos~ Schmid-RSS24-Khronos identifies changed objects through depth consistency, while OpenIN~ tang2025openin and DualMap~ jiang2025dualmap associate movable objects with supporting anchors to maintain object identities. However, these approaches primarily reason about scene changes at the object or relation level, without explicitly revising noisy or outdated points within each object instance. As a result, local artifacts introduced by perception errors or stale observations can remain embedded in the object representation, degrading long-term mapping quality. To address both dynamic environments and noisy perception, we propose an online refinable open-vocabulary semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object-centric maps over time. The key idea is to maintain a probabilistic confidence estimate for every object point, rather than treating integrated points as permanent entries. Each confidence score is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: points consistently supported by new observations are reinforced, while those inconsistent with segmentation masks, depth measurements, or visibility cues are progressively down-weighted and eventually removed. This enables semantic maps to preserve reliable geometry while eliminating perception artifacts and outdated points caused by object motion. To maintain consistent object identities, the framework further combines 2D tracking for in-view motion with feature-based re-identification after objects leave and re-enter the field of view, as shown in . To evaluate its effectiveness as an online spatial memory for autonomous robots, we integrate the proposed semantic mapping framework into a vision-language navigation (VLN) framework du2026vlnav and evaluate it on object navigation and embodied question answering tasks in real-world environments. The main contributions of this work are: We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework with point-level confidence updating, enabling object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. We introduce a multi-view temporal update mechanism that reinforces reliable object points while suppressing spurious and outdated points caused by perception errors and object motion, improving mapping accuracy and robustness in dynamic environments. We integrate object tracking and feature-based re-identification to preserve consistent object identities under motion and demonstrate the proposed map as an effective online spatial memory for vision-language navigation and embodied question answering. These approaches demonstrate the value of structured semantic memory for language-guided robotic reasoning. However, they mainly focus on semantic abstraction and typically assume that fused object points remain valid once inserted. As a result, erroneous or old points introduced by noisy perception or object motion are difficult to revise through later observations. title: Measuring the Reasoning-Action Coupling in Driving Vision-Language-Action Models through Counterfactuals
summary: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models bring an appealing form of explainability to a safety-critical domain, since a system that can state the reasons for its maneuvers offers the transparency that deployment and public trust in autonomous driving demand. These models read the world into language before they act on it, describing the scene and reasoning over it in text that ranges from chain-of-thought to multi-stage question answering on the way to a trajectory. That framing quietly assumes two separable properties, namely that the trajectory follows the generated reasoning and that the generated reasoning tracks the causes that actually produce the trajectory. To thoroughly investigate these properties, we apply causal, counterfactual interventions to four driving VLAs across different benchmarks. First, we perturb the models' own reasoning and show that altering its meaning produces small trajectory changes relative to blanking the same models' camera inputs, a pattern that persists across benchmarks and model architectures. We then construct scene-level counterfactuals through photorealistic removal of key objects named in the models' reasoning and analyze whether the generated reasoning and trajectories track these changes. Overall, our findings indicate that the reasoning these models present to account for their resulting driving behavior is weakly coupled to that behavior itself, pointing to limits on the explainability these systems are intended to provide.

Introduction sec:intro An autonomous driving model that writes ``a pedestrian is entering the crosswalk, so I will slow down'' before emitting a trajectory is making a double promise about its generated . It claims that the stated reason contributes to the predicted maneuver, and that the pedestrian is a relevant cause of the vehicle slowing down. Most driving vision--language--action (VLA) models make some version of this promise. The text they emit ranges from multi-step chains of thought zhou2025autovla,yuan2025autodrive and single-sentence chains of causation wang2025alpamayo to question--answer exchanges about the scene tian2024drivevlm,sima2024drivelm . Across these systems, generated is presented as a means of explaining driving decisions xu2023drivegpt4,hwang2024emma,jiang2024senna,yuan2025autodrive,chi2025impromptu,hu2025vla . Existing evaluations typically assess the generated text against reference answers and the predicted trajectory against a recorded future sima2024drivelm,tian2024drivevlm . High scores on these two outputs do not establish either that the trajectory depends on the content of the generated , or that the remains grounded in the visual evidence that it cites. A model can produce a plausible rationale while its trajectory follows shortcut priors, and it can receive strong scores under both separate text and trajectory evaluations. We therefore test two requirements implied by treating generated as an explanation of a driving action: 0.2em Does the trajectory of a driving VLA depend on the semantic content of the it generates, or merely accompany it? When the world a driving VLA sees is changed, does its generated and trajectory respond to this change? We answer these questions with two counterfactual interventions. For the first question, we keep the visual scene fixed, edit the model's own generated , and decode the resulting trajectory under the same inference configuration. For the second, we remove a model-identified action-relevant object from the camera frames and rerun inference, allowing the model to generate a new and trajectory from the edited visual input. The -side intervention tests whether the stated reasoning steers the action. The image-side intervention tests whether this object-level change in visual evidence affects the model's generated and its trajectory. Within this image-side comparison, observing the regenerated and trajectory together reveals whether a revision to the model's stated reason is accompanied by a corresponding trajectory response, separating models that update both reasoning and action from those that update only one output. Two calibrations make intervention responses comparable across models. Each -side edit is paired within scene with a semantic-control paraphrase, so a model that reacts to any token-level change is not mistaken for a model that reacts to changed meaning. We additionally report each intervention response relative to the model's response to camera blanking, which provides a model-specific reference scale for visual sensitivity. Applied to four driving VLAs on two benchmarks ( sec:setup ), our thorough evaluations return a consistent picture of a weak coupling between a driving VLA's reasoning and action while also uncovering different model-specific shortcomings in their explainability. title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
summary: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

Blocking action attention to both signal groups (w/o ) preserves signal quality but reduces task completion to near the action-only baseline. Allowing direct SS--FS attention (Full Attention) reduces frame-level accuracy and task completion while preserving strong trajectory-level performance. This qualitative intervention shows that status inputs can directly steer action generation toward corrective behavior, supporting their use for biasing the policy toward adjustment and recovery when needed. Effect of Failure Data Quantity sec:failure_data_scaling On Insert Flower, we vary the number of terminal-failure trajectories using nested subsets of 50, 120, 190, and 250 trajectories, with 250 used in the main experiments. The other three data types, training settings, and failure-data sampling proportion remain fixed. Thus, larger subsets provide more diverse failure examples without increasing their share of training samples. Figure~ fig:failure_data_scaling shows that frame-level status prediction improves as the failure dataset grows, while task-completion scores remain broadly stable. This is consistent with the role of terminal-failure data: they supervise the distinction between terminal failure and successful completion, while their actions are excluded from imitation. Broader coverage of terminal-failure states thus enriches status supervision without directly supplying additional corrective actions. The stable completion scores are also consistent with adjustment and recovery depending primarily on the pre-intervention and recovery data held fixed in this experiment. Pre-intervention failures supervise signals at recoverable errors, while recovery demonstrations provide corrective actions. Together, these observations support the complementary roles of terminal-failure supervision and recovery-related data. Echo also achieves 89.97 frame-level status accuracy. These results complement the real-world findings with a simulation evaluation of task completion and status prediction. title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: \textit{can a VLA's own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution?} Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA $π_{0.5}$ and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have made strong progress toward the goal of generalist, language-conditioned robot policies. Models such as ~ intelligence2025pi05 and GR00T~ nvidia2025gr00t can execute diverse, multi-stage manipulation tasks across a variety of tasks and embodiment and, especially after task-specific fine-tuning, can achieve relatively high mutli-task success rates. However, even well-trained policies still experience a wide variety of failure modes, (e.g., poor language grounding kwok2026cover , deadlocks, and mistakes gu2025safe ) which are often sudden and difficult to predict. A natural framework for addressing such failure modes during deployment is runtime monitoring: using an external verifier or monitor to detect when the policy's execution is straying from typical/successful deployment. Existing approaches obtain this monitoring signal from several sources. Sentinel~ agia2024sentinel uses an external VLM, along with an action consistency heuristic, to judge when the policy is failing to make progress on a particular task. Generalist reward models, such as Robometer~ liang2026robometer , learn to judge task progress from datasets of robot videos. Other methods instead use policy internals directly for failure detection. For example, SAFE~ gu2025safe trains a failure classifier to predict rollout success directly from policy activations, while FIPER~ romer2025failure combines an internal-based anomaly score and an uncertainty metric over actions to flag anomalous rollouts. In this work, we investigate a different use of policy internals for runtime monitoring. Specifically, we build on recent successes in mechanistic interpretability for VLAs~ buurmeijer2026observing, lu2025probing , which demonstrated that the activations of the VLM backbone contain easily-decodable representations of task-relevant features such as end-effector pose, object states, and task phase. We hypothesize that a VLA's internal activations may also encode task progress: how far the policy has progressed through a task. In successful executions, progress advances predictably over time (monotonically decreasing), while in suboptimal or failed executions, the progress probe falls behind the elapsed time. Furthermore, task progress can be learned entirely from successful executions and can be labeled without human supervision. We propose progress probes---linear decodings from the VLA's activations to task progress---as lightweight internal-based runtime monitors. We study progress probes by training them on the intelligence2025pi05 VLA using a dataset of success-only task executions. At deployment, runtime monitoring consists of taking the VLA's internal activations (that are already computed as part of the forward pass of inference), passing them through the linear progress probe, and measuring the deviation between the current estimated task progress and the expected task progress computed from successful demonstrations. Not only does our probe-based monitor require only successful data for training, but it also runs between and faster than an external foundation-model monitor. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, we find that linear probes can indeed accurately predict task progress for demonstrations, and that they provide an effective signal for detecting unsuccessful policy rollouts. Our monitor achieves competitive or superior failure detection performance with both Robometer and SAFE baselines, while providing fast inference and requiring only successful demonstrations for training. This result indicates that even when VLAs fail to generate successful actions, their activations still retain information useful for detecting task progress and failure, which can be obtained using a simple linear readout. Specifically, our contributions are as follows: We demonstrate empirically that linear probes trained over demonstration data can accurately decode task progress from vision-language representations, across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks. We develop a minimalist progress-based runtime monitor which uses these probes to detect deviations from expected progress at runtime, without failure data or an external VLM. We evaluate our monitor on 6 VLABench tasks and 6 real-world manipulation tasks, achieving AUROC scores of 0.788 and 0.78 respectively, matching or exceeding competitive baselines including SAFE and Robometer. Related Work sec:relatedworks Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the behavior of neural networks by studying their internal representations and computations. Over the past decade, researchers in computer vision and language modeling have developed tools to understand what neurons learn and how semantic concepts and structured knowledge are encoded and used. One particularly exciting perspective is the linear representation hypothesis~ mikolov2013linguistic, park2024linear , which posits that high-level concepts are encoded as directions in activation space and that interventions along concept directions can steer model behavior~ zou2023representation . This allows one to connect the study of representations to their functional role and reveal behaviors not visible in model output hubinger2024sleeper, macdiarmid2024simple . More recently, researchers have extended similar ideas to robotic VLAs, investigating how their internal representations encode semantic concepts~ haon2025mechanistic , motion primitives~ swann2026sparse , and physical and relational states~ buurmeijer2026observing, lu2025probing . Our work contributes to this growing body of interpretability research on robotic VLAs by investigating whether linear probes trained only on successful demonstrations can extract a task progress signal from internal activations. Beyond decoding, we further show that this signal can be turned into a lightweight runtime monitor that detects departures from expected progress, demonstrating how VLA internals can support failure detection without an external foundation model. Learned robot policies, including VLAs, remain prone to unexpected failures during deployment, motivating techniques for monitoring policies at runtime and detecting failures as they occur. Existing runtime monitors differ primarily in the signals they use to recognize such failures. One approach is to use deviations from successful behavior, flagging observations or policy outputs that appear anomalous relative to successful executions xu2025can, romer2025failure . Another is to leverage an external evaluator, such as a VLM judge agia2024sentinel, kwok2025robomonkey, wu2025foresight or a learned failure predictor gu2025safe trained directly over policy internals. More general reward models can also serve as runtime monitors by recognizing abnormal task progression liang2026robometer . Overall, several design decisions remain open for runtime monitoring, including whether monitoring requires an external validator, whether it must be trained on failure data, and whether the policy's own representations provide useful signals for monitoring. We study the latter hypothesis by probing these representations for task progress and detecting failures when estimated progress deviates from the progression expected during successful execution. title: HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
summary: Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA's capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.
full_text: Introduction A long-standing goal in embodied intelligence is to build virtual embodied agents fung2025embodied that can operate in open-ended games under the same interaction constraints as human players. Achieving this goal requires two complementary capabilities: long-horizon autonomy to maintain goals and adapt plans; and reliable native-interface control to translate first-person visual observations into keyboard-and-mouse actions. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying these capabilities by combining partially observable, compositional tasks with diverse visuomotor interactions fan2022minedojo,zheng2023mcu . A generally capable Minecraft agent must therefore integrate long-horizon planning with native-interface execution in a closed loop, continually updating its decisions from visual feedback. Existing Minecraft agents have primarily emphasized one of these two capabilities. On the one hand, visuomotor policies and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models address native-interface control by directly mapping raw first-person observations to keyboard-and-mouse actions baker2022video,lifshitz2023steve,li2025jarvis . However, these models typically lack mechanisms for persistently tracking task state and explicitly reasoning over task dependencies, limiting their long-horizon autonomy. On the other hand, agents driven by large language models (LLMs) or vision-language models (VLMs) support long-horizon reasoning through task decomposition planning wang2023voyager,zhu2023ghost,wang2024jarvis,li2024optimus . However, many of these methods still rely on environment APIs, predefined skills, or functional actions for low-level execution, which may be unavailable in most games. Although recent work has begun to combine high-level planning with learned policies wang2025openha,park2025mrsteve , integrating task-state tracking, completion verification, and failure recovery remains an open challenge. Satisfying both requirements introduces coupled challenges at the planning and action timescales. At the planning timescale, long-horizon autonomy requires tracking the objective, progress, and execution history across subtasks, while ensuring that plans are consistent with Minecraft mechanics and remain within the lower-level policy's capabilities wang2023describe . The agent must also determine when to terminate the current subtask: terminating too early leaves the subtask unfinished, whereas terminating too late wastes actions and may even undo existing progress. At the action timescale, native-interface control requires a single VLA policy to operate reliably across heterogeneous task distributions. In particular, non-GUI control and GUI interaction differ in both visual distributions and mouse-action semantics: mouse movement rotates the camera in the former but displaces the cursor in the latter, making naive joint training susceptible to negative transfer he2026training,yang2026omniactor . Each VLA invocation must also be reliable, since even small per-subtask failure risks accumulate over repeated invocations in long-horizon tasks. To address these challenges, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent that combines a capability-aware harness for long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. At the slower planning timescale, we design the harness with a structured memory of task progress and a VLM planner that selects the next atomic subtask. To close the planning--execution loop, we introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. The harness then verifies the task state and decides whether to advance, recover, or replan. At the faster action timescale, the VLA predicts native keyboard-and-mouse actions from the subtask instruction and first-person visual observation. To mitigate negative transfer across heterogeneous interaction regimes, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings for non-GUI and GUI tasks. Following world knowledge injection and imitation learning, we further finetune the VLA through reinforcement learning (RL) to improve recovery when execution deviates from demonstration trajectories. We comprehensively evaluate HiSTEVE on atomic and long-horizon benchmarks. Compared with the strongest baseline in our main comparison, HiSTEVE improves average success by percentage points on MineStudio Bench and points on OpenHA, with family-level gains of up to points on LongBench. The largest long-horizon improvements occur in tasks requiring multi-stage resource production or the reuse of information gathered during exploration. Ablations reveal that stronger atomic execution alone does not yield comparable gains in long-horizon performance. With the VLA held fixed, the full harness more than doubles goal success relative to fixed-horizon handoff, highlighting the importance of organizing local execution around a persistent task state. The learned completion detector also outperforms prompted general-purpose VLMs, providing more accurate completion judgments to support this execution loop. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We present HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness, enabling HiSTEVE to maintain goals and adapt plans throughout long-horizon execution. We enable reliable native-interface control through regime-specific RMSNorm branches, separate mouse-movement token embeddings, and a three-stage training strategy. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance and can complete long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like a human player. title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
summary: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.

Introduction Many robotic tasks require agents to anticipate external environmental evolution to achieve precise control. This structure is particularly prominent in agile aerial robotics. A representative example is dynamic-gate racing with quadrotors kaufmann2018deep, song2022policy, romer2025flying , where the robot must predict the future motion of moving gates and generate accurate control commands to pass through narrow openings at high speed. Existing solutions song2022policy often address this challenge through modular pipelines that decouple prediction, planning, and control. Although such designs are interpretable and effective, they usually rely on task-specific engineering and optimize each module separately. World-model-based reinforcement learning hafner2019dream, hafner2020mastering provides an integrated alternative. By learning compact latent dynamics from interaction, methods such as Dreamer hafner2019dream can imagine future trajectories and optimize policies in latent space. However, in agile robotic control, a learned world model often has to capture both the evolution of the external environment and the robot's high-frequency rigid-body dynamics within the same learned rollout. This entangles two sources of dynamics with different structures: the external dynamics are partially observable and history-dependent, whereas the robot's internal dynamics are often smooth and available through physical modeling. As a result, policy optimization through purely learned rollouts may suffer from model bias and less accurate gradients for precise physical control. This motivates using differentiable simulation for the robot's physical motion, so that the learned world model can focus on latent external dynamics. Differentiable reinforcement learning (DiffRL) xu_accelerated_2022, mora2021pods offers a complementary direction. By backpropagating through a differentiable physical model, it can provide low-variance first-order gradients for policy optimization and be particularly effective for smooth robotic systems. However, differentiable RL alone typically assumes that the transition and reward structures are differentiable and explicitly available. This makes it difficult to handle partially observable external dynamics, moving targets with unknown future motion, and non-differentiable task events such as gate-crossing rewards. To address this problem, we propose DiffDreamer, which structurally separates robot dynamics from external environment dynamics and couples their rollouts for policy optimization. DiffDreamer synchronizes latent world-model imagination with differentiable physical rollouts: under the same action, the world model updates an implicit state representing external time-varying features, while the simulator propagates the explicit robot state. The actor receives both states as input, and its objective is decomposed into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. We compare DiffDreamer with RL, trajectory planning, and model predictive control (MPC) baselines on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, and demonstrate its effectiveness through transfer to real quadrotor flight. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 0pt 0pt We propose a dual-pathway policy optimization framework that synchronizes latent imagination with differentiable physical rollouts to improve optimization accuracy and reduce the burden of learning high-frequency robot dynamics within the world model. We conduct comprehensive experiments on two quadrotor tasks with dynamic external environments to validate the advantages of the proposed method in terms of control accuracy and predictive capabilities. We conduct ablation studies on reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representation to assess their contributions. We provide proof-of-concept validation of aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing in real-world scenarios. Related Work Agile Quadrotor Flight and Modular Pipelines Agile quadrotor flight, including autonomous racing, typically relies on modular pipelines for perception, state estimation, trajectory planning, and low-level control under tight real-time constraints~ hanover2024autonomous . In dynamic environments with moving targets or gates, these pipelines often use motion-prediction modules to support downstream planning and control. Representative approaches combine learned gate perception with trajectory generation and tracking~ kaufmann2018deep , learned data abstraction with nonlinear filtering and time-optimal planning~ foehn2022alphapilot , or model-predictive and time-optimal control for aggressive waypoint or gate traversal~ foehn2021time, romero2022model, krinner2024mpcc . Policy search can also tune model-predictive controllers for agile flight~ song2022policy . Elastic Tracker combines target-motion prediction with visibility-aware spatio-temporal trajectory optimization for aerial tracking~ ji2022elastic . These modular pipelines are effective and interpretable, especially when the environment structure and task objectives are well specified. However, their modules are usually designed and optimized separately, so prediction or planning errors may propagate to downstream control. Model-based Reinforcement Learning Model-based reinforcement learning uses learned or known dynamics models for planning and policy optimization, supporting sample-efficient end-to-end policy learning. Model-free methods learn directly from interaction with the environment and typically require more data~ schulman2017proximal, haarnoja2018soft . Classical and modern approaches have explored probabilistic dynamics and uncertainty-aware planning, such as PILCO and PETS deisenroth2011pilco,chua2018deep , short model-generated rollouts for value/policy learning, such as MBPO janner2019trust , and latent dynamics for planning or imagination-based actor-critic learning, such as MuZero, Dreamer, and TD-MPC schrittwieser2020mastering,hafner2019dream,hafner2020mastering,hafner2023mastering,hansen2022temporal,hansen2023td . Despite their sample efficiency, model-based methods remain sensitive to model fidelity, especially in high-accuracy and high-frequency robotic control m2023model . In agile quadrotor tasks, a single learned rollout must often capture both partially observable external motion and fast rigid-body dynamics, which introduces distinct learning challenges. title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
comment: 14 pages, 14 figures. Project website, open-source hardware and software, and demonstration videos: https://opentac.github.io
summary: We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold. First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force. Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole"). We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments. We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning on four real-world robot embodiments. Additionally, adaptive acquisition enables kilohertz-rate partial readouts, exceeding full-array raster scanning on the same sensor by 19.2X at 16 sampled taxels per update for a 1024-taxel skin. We provide all hardware, software, and result videos are at opentac.github.io
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction As robots expand to perform tasks in more general, varied, and dynamic environments, their ability to manipulate quickly, reliably, and safely will increasingly depend on directly sensing and reacting to contact---that is, on tactile sensing. However, sensors must first be customized to fit the end-effector or surface of interest. As a result, research on the use of tactile sensing is fundamentally limited by customizability: researchers must either adapt their work to sensors manufactured in fixed geometries, or they must possess sufficient design and fabrication expertise to develop custom sensors in-house. These constraints are particularly limiting when instrumenting custom-designed robot geometries or larger, irregular surfaces. In this paper, we focus on conformal tactile skins, as they integrate distributed sensing elements into thin, flexible surfaces that can be wrapped around robot geometries, enabling fully sensorized robot bodies. However, existing tactile skins, such as FlexiTac~ flexitac , provide only normal-force (1D) estimates and require manual redesign for each new geometry. We present a sensor design that can be easily customized to fit many robot geometries, scaled in sensing area or resolution, and used to estimate normal and shear forces (3D) over local groups of sensing elements. Several efforts have partially addressed sensor customizability and made tactile skins more capable and accessible for the robot control and learning communities ~ flexitac,anyskin,eflesh . AnySkin provides replaceable sensing surfaces but relies on a predefined electronic layout~ anyskin , while eFlesh automates the design of a deformable sensor body but relies on separately supplied magnetometer electronics~ eflesh . In addition to the challenges of customizing the entire sensor, existing sensors are sampled at rates ranging between 30 and 100 Hz. Such raster scanning-based acquisition can limit the ability to resolve and respond to contacts lasting only a few milliseconds. Beyond hardware, changes in sensor geometry must also be accommodated by the software used to acquire, simulate, and process tactile observations. To address these limitations, we introduce OpenTac, an open sensor design environment and software ecosystem for customizable, scalable tactile sensing (Fig.~ fig:overview ). OpenTac supports the design of low-cost piezoresistive tactile skins that estimate both local normal and shear forces with millimeter-scale spatial resolution over planar and developable surfaces. Our sensor combines a flexible printed circuit board and a piezoresistive film with a structured elastomeric overlay that redistributes lateral pressure across neighboring sensing elements, allowing local shear to be decoded while retaining normal-force information. The sensing layout, electrode geometry, and mechanical overlay can be customized to the surface geometry and force range of interest. =-1 To support this degree of customizability, OpenTac includes a full-stack ecosystem of design, simulation, and interoperability tools. OpenTac-CAD is a design tool that automatically generates sensor fabrication files from a desired geometry. Users can provide a 2D outline, select a developable surface on a 3D robot model, or specify an abstract verbal description, such as ``design a star-shaped sensor that fits inside a circle with a diameter 5~cm.'' In addition, OpenTac-CAD produces a machine-readable manifest file describing the sensor's geometry, electrical addressing, and mechanical configuration. OpenTac-Sim provides tools to simulate the sensors and sensor-object interactions for robot manipulation tasks across any sensor design described by the manifest file. OpenTac-Transfer enables cross-sensor transfer by mapping calibrated tactile observations across sensor layouts using their physical coordinates and local surface frames. These components allow sensors with different shapes, resolutions, and electrical layouts to share acquisition and processing tools and provide a common interface for downstream control and learning. =-1 Scaling tactile coverage also increases the number of measurements required to read the sensor. To address this, we also provide OpenTac-Xampling, an adaptive acquisition method which operates across different sensor outlines using adaptive partial scans. For example, on a skin, adaptive acquisition of sparse contact events reaches 1286 Hz, more than a 19 increase over full-array scans (67 Hz) achieved by conventional acquisition~ sundaram2019stag . =-1 We evaluate all components of the ecosystem. We use to generate fabrication files for more than 30 sensor layouts (including robot fingers, grippers, palms, and feet), fabricate the corresponding sensors, and deploy them on four real robot embodiments. We further evaluate the 3D force estimates against a commercial force/torque sensor. Finally, we demonstrate that our sensor's normal and shear force estimates enable contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning. To summarize, our main contributions are: OpenTac: a full-stack ecosystem for automated sensor design, fabrication, simulation, cross-sensor observation mapping, and kilohertz-rate adaptive acquisition. A customizable tactile skin that estimates normal and shear forces using a simple, scalable construction. =-1 Evaluations spanning over 30 fabricated layouts, sensor characterization, high-speed sensing, and real-world robot control and learning, demonstrating the utility of the resulting tactile observations for contact-rich manipulation. All hardware, software, and firmware is available under permissive licenses, enabling replication, modification, and redistribution for research and commercial use. Related Work sec:related_work =-1 Tactile sensing hardware typically involves optical, magnetic, capacitive, and/or resistive transduction to recover contact. GelSight provides high-resolution optical contact sensing~ gelsight , while uSkin integrates distributed three-axis force elements~ uskin . GelSlim uses marker displacements and inverse finite-element modeling to estimate dense contact forces~ ma2019denseforce , while Yan ~use a magnetized film to decouple normal force and one shear component~ yan2021magneticskin . Mechanical structures can also encode shear into differential pressure: Sun ~place a bump over four piezoresistive cells and infer load direction from their relative responses~ sun2019shear . builds on this principle using a single-FPCB (flexible PCB) sensing architecture designed for automated customization and shared readout design that specifies a unified cross-sensor interface. Early work on customizing and scaling tactile skins used modular or severable elements to cover complex robot surfaces~ ohmura2006,mittendorfer2011humanoid , while later systems such as the iCub skin, RobotSweater, and conformal tactile textiles target large-area conformable coverage~ icubskin,robotsweater,luo2021conformal . ReSkin and AnySkin decouple the replaceable magnetic interface from the electronics~ reskin,anyskin . eFlesh automates magnetic microstructures~ eflesh , and FlexiTac provides an open flexible pressure array~ flexitac . Computational design tools have also produced personalized FPCB tactile gloves~ murphy2025flexglove and surface-conforming capacitive sensors for existing 3D objects~ ilic2026retrofit . Lim ~use laser-patterned flexible circuits to integrate capacitive pressure and bending sensors with temperature and proximity modules in customizable multimodal skins~ lim2026scalable . instead starts from robot geometry and jointly generates the sensing layout, routing, connectorization, mechanical structure, and associated metadata, enabling robot-specific tactile skins. Tactile simulation and manipulation. TACTO~ tacto and Taxim~ taxim focus on simulating the imaging process inherent in vision-based tactile sensors. DiffTactile~ difftactile , TacEx~ tacex , and Taccel~ taccel additionally implement sensor surface deformation mechanics for robot manipulation. HydroShear further models shear and stick-slip effects for sim-to-real learning~ hydroshear . Tactile feedback has been used in fine manipulation and shear-based control~ 3dvitac,simshear . Different to prior work, implements a simulation framework specifically for sensors using the compiled sensor geometry and bump layout to generate normal and tangential deformation observations. Acquisition and cross-sensor representations. High-rate tactile sensing has used event-driven hardware~ NeuTouch,evetac and adaptive subsampling of dense arrays~ slepyan2024acts . applies adaptive sampling across arbitrary compiled layouts using manifest-defined valid regions and neighborhoods. Cross-sensor tactile representation learning combines aligned synthetic tactile data with real-world multimodal data to learn sensor-agnostic visuo-tactile representations~ sparsh, anytouch,pmlr-v306-zhang26gh . instead maps calibrated contact fields through physical coordinates and local frames, without needing paired cross-sensor data. The OpenTac Ecosystem sec:system OpenTac introduces a full-stack ecosystem for piezoresistive tactile skins in robot control and learning applications. The OpenTac tactile sensor comprises a structured deformable overlay, which redistributes tangential loading across a small grid of underlying taxels. This enables the estimation of both normal and shear forces over the piezoresistive film. All components use a shared sensor description: the manifest. The ecosystem comprises four distinct modules: , which designs a sensor given a 2D outline or a developable 3D shape, producing the fabrication files and the manifest; , a simulation toolkit built on MuJoCo to simulate sensor readings; , a module to enable cross-sensor geometry transfer; and , an adaptive readout module enabling kilohertz-rate sampling for sparse contact acquisition. Together, these enable to be directly deployed across highly versatile traditional, learning-based, and interactive robotics applications. : Normal and Shear Sensor design sec:sensing We choose piezoresistive sensing for its low material cost, simple readout circuitry, and compatibility with standard flexible-PCB (fPCB) fabrication. The OpenTac sensor stack (Fig.~ fig:cad B) comprises three primary components: a single fPCB (bottom), a piezoresistive film (middle), and a printed mechanical cover (top). At each row--column intersection on the fPCB, interdigitated copper fingers form one taxel. Any applied pressure on the sensor decreases the local resistance on the piezoresistive film and is converted by a readout circuit into an output voltage to estimate normal force. The top surface of the sensor is a deformable bump strip, based on~ bump-strip-reference , which is where sensor-object interactions occur. Each bump sits atop a small window (e.g., ) of taxels. For three-axis force sensing, each elastomeric bump covers a local group of taxels, with the number and arrangement of taxels determined by the sensor geometry. Tangential loading tilts the bump, resulting in a pressure, and by extension, resistance differential across the underlying taxels, producing differential responses and . Optionally, we may use an affine map to calibrate sensor readings to force units . The manifest defines the grouping and signs for each compiled array. This design choice enables a high degree of customization, by leveraging automated CAD and circuit design principles to parametrize sensor density, electrode layout, and mechanical transduction, while retaining the sensing, assembly, and readout processes. : Automatic sensor design sec:workflo

title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models

summary: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.

Introduction sec:1 In robotic control, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have rapidly advanced by leveraging semantic knowledge and generalization capabilities acquired through large-scale vision-language pretraining for robot action generation~ [1],[2],[3],[4],[5] . More recently, research has increasingly explored leveraging future dynamics and predictive and spatiotemporal priors acquired through video pretraining for action prediction and planning~ [6],[7],[8],[9],[10],[11] . In particular, diffusion/flow-based generative video models have emerged as key pretrained backbones for these approaches, as they can directly generate future visual dynamics~ [25],[26],[27],[28] . This growing reliance on pretrained video models makes it increasingly important to determine whether they have learned the physical dynamics required for robotic control. To this end, various benchmarks and evaluation methods have been proposed to assess intuitive physics, physical plausibility, and motion consistency in input or generated videos~ [31],[32],[35],[36],[37],[38],[46] . In parallel, probing studies have investigated the physical information encoded within pretrained video models~ [39],[41],[44],[45] . This line of work has also extended beyond encoder-based representation models to the intermediate denoising representations of diffusion-based video generators, showing that physics-related information can be decoded from pretrained representations. However, these approaches primarily focus on predefined physical labels, model-level preferences, or physics-related signals encoded in intermediate representations. Even when a physical inconsistency can be detected, they provide limited insight into which history-conditioned physical expectation conflicts with the observed behavior. More fundamentally, physical consistency is not a static visual property of individual frames, but a temporal property that emerges from changes in object identity, state, motion, and interaction across time. Sparse or short observations may therefore miss brief violations or lack the context needed to determine what should have occurred. Likewise, a single plausibility score cannot reveal where the expected and observed dynamics begin to diverge. Evaluating physical consistency thus requires continuously relating local observations to the physical expectations established by their temporal history. Rather than probing intermediate representations, a natural alternative is to directly ask a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to assess physical plausibility from video. However, Pixels to Principles~ [48] reports near-chance performance of recent MLLMs in challenging intuitive-physics settings on GRASP~ [49] and IntPhys 2~ [32] , despite physics-related cues being recoverable from their visual representations. Similarly, QuantiPhy~ [50] shows that, in quantitative kinematic inference from video, multimodal models often rely on pretrained world knowledge rather than faithfully integrating visual evidence with the provided physical prior. These findings suggest that current MLLMs are unreliable as direct judges of physical validity. Beyond this paradigm, recent work has explored leveraging predictive dynamics and spatiotemporal priors learned from video for robot policy learning. VPP~ [6] extracts predictive visual representations from a video diffusion model for action prediction without explicit future visual rollouts. More direct approaches, including World Action Models (WAMs) and related world-model-based policies, couple future prediction with action generation or planning~ [7],[8],[9],[10],[11] . EVA~ [9] generates future visual rollouts and uses an inverse dynamics model to derive executable actions and provide an executability signal for aligning the video world model. Cosmos Policy~ [10] generates actions as latent frames and predicts future states and values for model-based planning, whereas V-JEPA2-AC~ [11] predicts action-conditioned future states in latent space for planning. Despite their architectural differences, these approaches share the goal of exploiting predictive dynamics learned from video as priors for robot control. Pretrained Video World Models as Policy Priors sec:2.2 Prior work has explored different classes of video models for learning representations and dynamics relevant to robot control. Self-supervised video representation models learn temporal structure without explicit robot actions. V-JEPA2~ [11] follows a latent predictive objective, while VideoMAE V2~ [22] learns general spatiotemporal representations through masked video reconstruction. A separate line of work develops robot-specific, action-conditioned world models. DreamDojo~ [23] , for example, learns interaction dynamics from large-scale human videos and is subsequently adapted to generate future visual states conditioned on robot actions. Another line of work builds general-purpose generative video models, such as Stable Video Diffusion~ [25] , Wan~ [26] , and the Cosmos-Predict family~ [27],[28],[29] . These diffusion/flow-based models directly generate temporally evolving visual sequences and have increasingly been repurposed as pretrained backbones for representation-based policies and WAMs~ [6],[7],[8],[10] . Specifically, we evaluate Wan2.1, whose pretrained video backbone is adopted by DreamZero~ [8] , and Cosmos-Predict2, which is adapted for visuomotor control and planning in Cosmos Policy~ [10] . Among them, IntPhys2~ [32] evaluates four intuitive-physics principles---permanence, immutability, spatio-temporal continuity, and solidity---through video-level discrimination between physically possible and impossible events. However, it does not provide temporal annotations indicating when a physical violation occurs. To evaluate temporal localization, we introduce IntPhys2-Timing, which augments impossible videos with temporal annotations of their physical violations. title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success

summary: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.

title: RecallGS: Geometry-Grounded Recall for Online Semantic Gaussian Splatting
summary: Online semantic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables open-vocabulary scene understanding from streaming observations. However, existing methods recover geometric context missing from image-derived semantic features using an additionally learned 3D network, incurring extra training and runtime overhead. We observe that such geometric-semantic evidence may already exist in the agent's observation history and can be retrieved rather than learned. Based on this insight, we introduce RecallGS (Geometry-Grounded Recall for Online Semantic Gaussian Splatting), a lightweight, training-free mechanism that treats past observations as a non-parametric geometric-semantic prior. RecallGS follows a recall-ground-fuse pipeline: CLIP retrieves relevant observations, alpha-compositing weights identify geometrically supported views, and aggregate their semantic features over each Gaussian's rendered footprint. On ScanNet and ScanNet++, RecallGS achieves strong semantic segmentation performance at 2.48 FPS, demonstrating that geometric-semantic context can be effectively recovered from observation history without an additional learned 3D branch.

Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an efficient explicit representation for real-time novel-view synthesis kerbl20233d . Recent works extend 3DGS with open-vocabulary semantics by distilling vision-language features into Gaussians, either through rendering-based supervision qin2024langsplat,shi2024legaussians,zhou2024feature3dgs or direct 3D feature lifting and referring wu2024opengaussian,kim2025drsplat . This paradigm has further expanded to online embodied settings, using either language-aware 3DGS-SLAM katragadda2025onlinelangsplat,zhou2025ea3d or generalizable feed-forward reconstruction lee2026embodiedsplat , alongside online 3D instance segmentation methods that fuse 2D foundation-model predictions into persistent 3D representations xu2024embodiedsam,tang2025onlineanyseg . Despite this progress, existing online semantic 3DGS pipelines recover the geometric context missing from image-derived language features through an additional learned 3D branch, rather than directly reusing geometric-semantic evidence from past observations. EmbodiedSplat lee2026embodiedsplat , for instance, complements its 2D CLIP features radford2021learning with geometry-aware 3D features produced by passing the local Gaussian point cloud through a sparse 3D U-Net choy20194d equipped with a temporal memory adapter xu2024memoryadapters . This 3D branch, however, must be trained on large-scale posed 3D indoor scene data, which is costly to collect and introduces additional GPU-memory consumption and latency that directly reduce the online reconstruction speed. EmbodiedSplat-fast removes the 3D U-Net and memory adapter, increasing throughput from 0.75 FPS to 5.18 FPS at the cost of geometric-semantic context. This highlights the training and inference overhead of recovering explicit 3D context through an additional learned branch. We ask whether such context must be learned at all, or can instead be recovered from the agent's observation history. We observe that this trade-off is a consequence of treating each observation independently. An embodied agent operates in a persistent environment: a Gaussian that is geometrically or semantically ambiguous from the current viewpoint may correspond to a physical surface already observed earlier under a more favorable viewpoint, illumination, or occlusion pattern. This suggests that part of the geometric prior EmbodiedSplat's 3D branch must learn from parameters could instead be recovered from the agent's own trajectory, treating its accumulated observation history as a non-parametric geometric-semantic prior queried on demand rather than compressed once and discarded. However, effectively reusing past observations introduces several challenges. First, semantic similarity does not imply physical correspondence: a CLIP-based retrieval system radford2021learning may return frames containing a visually similar object-another chair, table, or door-at an entirely different location. Second, a Gaussian may project inside a historical image but still be occluded by closer geometry. Sampling the projected pixel would then transfer features from the occluder rather than from the queried surface. Finally, exhaustively verifying every historical camera against every incoming frame would itself undermine the efficiency this history is meant to provide, as a long-running agent may accumulate hundreds to thousands of observations. The problem is therefore not retrieval of similar-looking memories, but memory routing: determining, without prior semantic knowledge of the current Gaussians, which past observations should be allowed to influence each one. To this end, we propose RecallGS (Geometry-Grounded Recall), a lightweight mechanism requiring no additional training that treats an agent's observation history as a queryable source of geometric-semantic evidence, routed to the current Gaussians through a recall–ground–replay pipeline. Our contributions are threefold: (1) semantic recall, a cheap CLIP-based retrieval stage that narrows an unbounded observation history to a small candidate pool of appearance-plausible frames; (2) geometric grounding, which reranks these candidates using alpha-compositing weights to identify views that geometrically support the current Gaussians; and (3) compositing fusion, which reuses the same alpha-compositing weights to aggregate historical features over each Gaussian's full rendered footprint. Our experiments show that each component contributes independently to semantic accuracy, and that their combination enables effective geometric-semantic reasoning from observation history while maintaining efficient online inference Our contributions are as follows: We show that an agent's observation history can serve as a non-parametric geometric-semantic prior, providing complementary semantic evidence without additional 3D training or per-scene optimization. We propose RecallGS, a training-free recall-ground-fuse framework that efficiently retrieves relevant past observations, grounds them against the current geometry, and fuses their semantic evidence into the current Gaussians. We validate the contribution of each component and show that exploiting observation history consistently improves online semantic 3DGS while maintaining efficient inference. Related Work Language-Embedded Gaussian Splatting Building on 3D Gaussian Splatting kerbl20233d , one line of work embeds open-vocabulary semantics onto Gaussians via per-scene optimization, either by distilling 2D vision-language features through differentiable rendering supervision qin2024langsplat,shi2024legaussians,zhou2024feature3dgs or by directly associating semantic features with 3D structure through clustering, feature lifting, or compact Gaussian-level representations~ wu2024opengaussian,kim2025drsplat,li2025instancegaussian,cheng2025occamlgs,cen2025saga,qiu2024gls,shorinwa2024fastsplat . These methods establish 3DGS as an effective carrier of language features and improve their spatial consistency, instance awareness, or representation efficiency. However, most construct semantic fields specifically for each scene, which limits their applicability when observations arrive continuously. To remove scene-specific optimization, a class of feed-forward methods predicts 3D Gaussian representations directly from input images without per-scene training. This paradigm was established by geometric backbones such as pixelSplat charatan2024pixelsplat and MVSplat chen2024mvsplat , which regress RGB Gaussians from sparse image pairs. Building on this feed-forward formulation, subsequent work adds an open-vocabulary semantic branch: LSM fan2024lsm jointly regresses geometry, appearance, and semantics from unposed image pairs by lifting a pre-trained 2D language-based segmentation model into a 3D-consistent feature field decoded into semantic Gaussians, SLGaussian chen2025slgaussian targets the sparse-view regime with a multi-view language memory bank that maps high-dimensional CLIP features to compact per-object IDs for fast open-vocabulary querying, and SemanticSplat li2025semanticsplat further improves language-aware feed-forward reconstruction by fusing SAM~ kirillov2023segment and CLIP-LSeg~ li2022language features into a cost-volume representation for cross-view semantic aggregation. These approaches avoid per-scene semantic optimization and generalize across scenes, but still operate on a fixed, small set of input views rather than maintaining a persistent semantic representation under a streaming observation sequence. Online Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction and Segmentation A separate line of work extends 3DGS to the online setting required by embodied perception. Within visual SLAM, SplaTAM~ keetha2024splatam and Gaussian Splatting SLAM~ matsuki2024gsslam use explicit Gaussians for incremental tracking, mapping, and rendering, demonstrating that 3DGS can serve as a persistent scene representation under streaming observations. Building on this formulation, Online-LangSplat~ katragadda2025onlinelangsplat and EA3D~ zhou2025ea3d inject language or foundation-model features into the online reconstruction loop. Online-LangSplat's language module itself runs in milliseconds, but the overall SLAM-GS pipeline remains bottlenecked by per-frame camera-pose optimization, yielding well under 2 FPS end-to-end; EA3D similarly relies on a recurrent joint optimization module to align geometric and semantic features, at a comparable throughput cost. In parallel, online 3D instance segmentation methods incrementally fuse 2D foundation-model predictions into temporally consistent 3D instances~ xu2024embodiedsam,tang2025onlineanyseg , building on adapter-based caching mechanisms that aggregate RGB-D features frame-by-frame to endow otherwise-offline backbones with temporal learning ability~ xu2024memoryadapters ; these methods, however, operate on point-based representations rather than a differentiable and renderable Gaussian semantic field. Closest to our setting are online, generalizable feed-forward pipelines that avoid per-scene optimization entirely. FreeSplat++~ wang2025freesplat++ targets efficient whole-scene indoor reconstruction from long image sequences, using a low-cost cross-view aggregation module and a pixel-wise triplet fusion strategy to incrementally merge overlapping Gaussian primitives across views, together with a weighted floater-removal step that exploits the accumulated blending weights from this fusion. EmbodiedSplat~ lee2026embodiedsplat extends this backbone with open-vocabulary semantics through a sparse CLIP codebook and a learned 3D U-Net branch that injects geometric context into image-derived semantic features. This improves geometric-semantic awareness but requires additional 3D training and incurs non-negligible inference overhead. In contrast, we recover complementary geometric-semantic evidence directly from the agent's own observation history and route it to the current Gaussians through a lightweight recall-ground-fuse mechanism without an additional learned 3D semantic branch. title: PiHand: Latent Hand-Object Interaction Priors for Physics-Based Policy Learning
summary: Synthesizing physically grounded dexterous hand-object interactions is important for VR/AR, gaming, and robotics, yet remains challenging because subtle contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, and target trajectories must be jointly respected while maintaining natural grasps. Existing methods either track mocap trajectories with limited transfer to novel objects, or rely on hand-only generative priors that fail to capture coupled hand-object motion, sacrificing contact fidelity and sample efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PiHand, a Physically grounded Interaction-aware Hand motion synthesis framework. PiHand first trains expert policies that track mocap demonstrations in simulation, distills them into a unified hand-object interaction prior using a goal-conditioned VAE, and finally solve diverse dexterous manipulation tasks through bounded residual exploration in its latent space. With only a single reward and no complex curriculum training, this yields general tabletop manipulation policies that generalize to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB. The same prior transfers to object catching and bimanual handover, two tasks that are rarely seen in its training data. Across all tasks, PiHand consistently outperforms baselines in all metrics. We will release the processed data and model checkpoints.

Introduction sec:intro Generating realistic hand-object interactions is a foundational challenge in computer vision and graphics, with implications for VR/AR, gaming and robotics. Several kinematic approaches cha2024text2hoi, Muchen_LatentHOI, zhang2025bimart have made significant strides in generating such interactions from visual or textual inputs, yet they frequently suffer from noticeable physical implausibilities which make them unfit for deployment in simulated environments or on real-world robots. To bridge this gap, the robotics and physics-based animation communities have focused on learning generative control policies to synthesize the complex motions required to stably grasp and manipulate objects based on their geometry and target trajectory inside simulation. Yet this remains challenging because contact dynamics are subtle and discrete, objects vary widely in geometry and affordances, and the hand must continuously adapt its grasp and contact configuration to remain both natural-looking and physically correct.
